title: Show HN: Skillset: Easily curate and install agent skills collection
author: itsmeyaw
body: Hi everyone!Installing skills globally in ~/.agents or ~/.claude consumes too much context, yet manually installing specific skills for every project is tedious. Wouldn't it be better to group skills for programming, backend architecture, or graphic design into collections, and install them with a single command only when needed?To solve this, I built Skillset. It acts as a wrapper around the Vercel Skill CLI that batch-installs sets of skills from multiple sources using a single JSON file, essentially npm for skills!While similar tools exist, most are written from scratch, which makes me concerned about their compatibility. Because Vercel’s Skill CLI is already the de facto standard (imo!), Skillset uses it directly as an underlying library. So it guarantees seamless compatibility across teams, regardless of whether they use Skillset or the standard Vercel CLI.

title: Show HN: Minea – a Mac assistant that never steals your cursor (36-min raw run)
author: sujisss
body:
MINEA — the Mac secretary that acts before you ask

# It acts before you ask

 It keeps an eye on your screen, mail and messages, and when there's something worth doing it does it first. What you wondered about out loud, it builds a curriculum and teaches you. 

 Fixed (v1.1.4). Outgoing calls hadn't rung for nearly a month, and when they did you couldn't hear a thing. Both fixed. The build that wouldn't launch (Oct 3–23) is fixed too. You get the build that matches your chip, automatically. 

29 seconds · has sound · the on-screen captions are in Korean

## It doesn't only help while you're at the desk

A secretary that lives inside a window stops existing the moment you walk away.

It calls you

When an appointment is coming up, it calls first. If you went to bed late, it pushes the wake-up call back 30 minutes — unless something is scheduled after it, in which case it wakes you anyway. Pick up and you can talk: ask "what time was that meeting again?" and it answers; say "okay, got it" and it hangs up.

Hand work off from the lock screen

Say "Hey Siri, MINEA" or type it into the app, and your Mac does the work. The screen goes dark while it runs, and a notification wakes you when it's done.

It reads your Apple Watch as a trend, not a day

It isn't looking for a day that spikes — it's looking for the slow slide. When your health declines, no single day crosses a threshold, so a day-by-day check never catches it. It does not diagnose — it only says "this is different from your usual," and writes it down so you have an answer when a doctor asks "since when?"

It puts text on Meta Ray-Ban Display lenses

Silent, so you can use it around other people. Ask "what does this say?" and it reads back what you're looking at.

## It teaches what you wondered about

An answer only lasts for the moment. To make it stick, it has to be taught.

"Isn't adding English support just a setting you flip?"

↓ it doesn't let a passing question pass

 It builds a curriculum. The subject decides how many sessions and how long — one English expression gets 15 minutes, data modelling gets 50. It finds the empty slots, puts them in your calendar, and the window opens on the hour. 

It tests you first

Before session one there's a 20-minute diagnostic. Not just what you know — it reports on how you isolate a problem, how you transfer it, and your instincts. Every score comes with a reason, and if it can't give one it leaves the score blank. The reasoning questions are written so that you can solve them knowing nothing about the subject — if a beginner gets everything wrong and lands a "logic: 1," that's not a diagnosis, it's a label.

Seven minutes of feedback at the end

It tells you honestly how the session went. To keep it from inventing praise, it cites only what was actually said that day — "you asked twice whether the rest keeps running when one fails." If you barely spoke, it says that instead.

Then an exam, and one retry if you fail

Pass and your level in that field goes up a notch, and the next subject starts from there. Fail and you get one make-up session. There is no third — chasing you past that isn't help, it's collections.

## It moves even when nothing comes in

Most assistants need an input to react to. So on a quiet day they do nothing at all.

It asks "what's missing?" as a separate question

If it sees you've been lying down for two hours, it puts 30 minutes of yoga in an empty slot two hours out. If lunchtime has passed and it hasn't seen you eat, it places a meal slot. It doesn't speak — it just places the slot, which you're free to ignore or delete.

It clears away what it placed once the time passes

Seeing the workout you skipped again tomorrow morning is a debt notice. It reschedules once within the same day, and if there's nowhere to put it, it deletes it. Appointments you made yourself are never touched, even after they pass.

It leaves each day as a single page

Raw logs are heavy, so you end up never reading them. It writes an A5 page of a diary instead, and pulls the patterns out of what accumulates to justify what it does next.

It trusts what it observes over what you wrote down

If your Apple Watch says "bedtime 10pm" but you actually sleep at 3am, it moves the baseline. But only one step per day (45 minutes for bedtime), it records why it moved, and it tells you once that it moved.

## And on the Mac, this is what runs

Leave it on and it works without being told.

It keeps reading your mail and messages

New ones get read immediately, and appointments, deadlines and things needing a reply get pulled out. "I'll look at it later" stops happening.

It watches your screen and speaks first

If there's something to do on the screen you're looking at, a small bubble appears. Click it and it's done; ignore it and it disappears.

It creates, moves and deletes events and reminders directly

Connected to Calendar, Reminders and Google Calendar both ways. "Push that appointment back" is enough.

You can hand it work while you're out

From your iPhone, or through Telegram — the Mac does it for you.

It picks up where your old AI left off

Export your conversations from ChatGPT or Claude and drop them in — it reads them and starts already knowing what you're working on. (once is enough)

## You decide how far it goes

The more a thing acts on its own, the clearer its stopping points have to be.

| Calendar, notes, tidying | Done without asking. These are reversible. |
| --- | --- |
| Replies and sending mail | Drafted only. You read it and press send yourself. |
| Payments and bookings | It stops right before. A person always presses the last button. |
| Someone it hasn't dealt with | It asks you first. |

You can widen or narrow this in settings. The default is the cautious side.

## When it speaks first

It doesn't ask you things. It only surfaces quietly when the work is already visible.

A mail says "next Tuesday at 3" Tuesday 3pm meeting — want it in the calendar?

A message from three days ago still has no reply I've drafted a reply. Want to see it?

20 minutes before an appointment, time to leave You need to leave by two. It's a 35-minute trip.

 While you're reading news, watching a video or writing code, it doesn't speak. It also skips ad deadlines, things already finished, and things it already handled. 

 The biggest thing I learned building it: if interrupting is the only channel you have, you end up passive. When ringing is the only option, you weigh "is this worth a ring?" every single time — and eventually you say nothing at all. Only after adding a layer that doesn't ring (quietly placing things in the calendar) could it look after things often. 

## When you want to ask it directly

### Type @미네아 anywhere

Notes, a mail compose field, a messenger — anywhere you can type.

@minea write an autumn greeting message to my client

↓ a bubble appears a moment later

Autumn greeting ✓

 Click the bubble and the result is copied. Paste it right where you were typing. 

 Type @minea — case doesn't matter. @MINEA and the Korean @미네아 work too. Everything else — the app window, the iPhone app, Telegram and phone calls — takes plain English. 

The same words work on the phone and over a call.

 call me in 30 minutes push tomorrow's 2pm back what's on today? draft a polite reply to this mail 

## What it sees is filtered inside this computer

It's an app that watches your screen, your messages and your body, so here is exactly what goes where.

| Deciding whether to speak | A small model inside this Mac does it. Screen contents never leave the machine. |
| --- | --- |
| Messages and mail | A model on this computer reads all of it and only a few filtered lines leave. Anything from a bank, brokerage or card company isn't looked at at all, and account, card and ID numbers are masked before anything is passed on. |
| When it actually works | Only at that moment, and only the text that job needs, passes through a server. |
| Storage | Screenshots are not stored. Only what you asked for stays on this Mac. |
| Accounts | There is no sign-up. It doesn't take your name or your email address. |

## Setup

Two permissions have to be turned on — it has to see the screen and click on your behalf.

1. Open the downloaded file and drag it to Applications Drag the MINEA icon onto the folder.

If nothing happens when you click Download — Safari is asking “Do you want to allow downloads?” Click Allow. The file is hosted on GitHub, so Safari asks once

If macOS says the app “is damaged and can’t be opened,” you have a build older than 1.1.0 — that was our bug and it is fixed. Download again
2. Turn on Screen Recording A dialog appears the first time you open it. If it doesn't, enable MINEA here.

System Settings › Privacy & Security › Screen Recording
3. Turn on Accessibility Needed so it can click for you.

System Settings › Privacy & Security › Accessibility
4. Restart the app Permissions only take effect after a restart. After that it stays up on its own.
5. To let it watch on its own — press setup once The setup button downloads the 5.2GB judgement model — it starts working once that is down, and the better model keeps coming in the background. Ten minutes to an hour depending on your connection, and you only download it once. You see a progress bar. No Homebrew, no password.

Skip it and @minea still works — only the watching-on-its-own part stays off
6. If you also want the iPhone and Apple Watch Turn on "Phone connection" in settings and a six-digit number appears. Enter it in the iPhone app and you're done, once and for all. Calls, health and lock-screen hand-off start working from then on.
7. If you want it to handle the web too — the Chrome extension Sign in to claude.ai in Chrome and install the extension, and it will click through websites for you. If you choose "Hide My Email" during Apple sign-in it becomes a different account and won't connect.

claude.ai/chrome · quit and reopen Chrome after installing

 If you use the Claude desktop app — while it's running it takes over the Chrome extension connection. Quit the Claude app when you want MINEA to do web work. (If you don't use web work, it doesn't matter.) 

 Even with the permissions on, screen contents never leave this Mac. Whether to speak up is decided inside this computer. 

## Once it's running, this is the speed

Deciding whether to speak up happens inside this Mac. That's why it's fast, and why it costs nothing.

| When you ask | Ask it something on a call and it answers in 2–4 seconds. Measured, not estimated — "what time is it?" 3.8s · "what's on today?" 1.8s. |
| --- | --- |
| Looking at your screen | Say "what's this?" and it reads what you're looking at and answers in 2 seconds. The image is never stored. Only what you asked for is kept. |
| Whether to speak up | It reads your mail, messages and screen and decides inside this Mac. Nothing leaves, and it costs nothing. |
| When something does leave | Only when you actually hand it work. Judgement, screen reading and call answers all stay on this Mac. |
| Space | App 192–364MB + judgement model 5.2GB (growing to a better 15GB as you use it). The model downloads once. Skip the model and handing it work with @minea still works. |
| When the Mac sleeps | It stops. Close the lid and nothing happens until you open it — saying it plainly rather than hiding it. This is the biggest limitation right now. |

## It's a trial for now

| Free | If you have a Claude account you can use it without a limit through that. If you don't, you get 30 runs to try it. No card needed. Signing in also runs it on a stronger model — the same setup the author uses. The free runs are a taste, one tier below (they still get dates right). |
| --- | --- |
| One thing to say up front | The 30 free runs come out of an allowance I've paid for in advance. I build and pay for this alone, so if a lot of people arrive at once that allowance can run out and the trial may pause or stop. If that happens I'll write it here and reopen it as I refill. Using your own Claude account isn't affected — that path doesn't touch my allowance. |
| After that | Pricing isn't decided yet. I'd rather hear from people who've used it first. |
| What you need | A Mac — Apple Silicon (M1 and later) and Intel both. macOS 11 (Big Sur) or later. Calls, Apple Watch and the glasses need the iPhone app, which is open on TestFlight — iOS 16 or later. |
| The first time | Once installed you can start asking right away — type @minea … in any text field. To let it watch your mail and screen on its own, press the setup button in the app once. That downloads the model (5.2GB) that decides, inside this Mac, whether to speak up. It works as soon as that is down — the better model follows in the background, and the app moves up to it on its own. No Homebrew, no password. Once is enough, and you see a progress bar while it downloads. |
| Language | The whole interface is in English — and so is everything it says to you: calls, tutoring, the daily page, the nudges. If your Mac is set to English it comes up in English on its own; switch it at the top of settings and it changes immediately, no restart. Being straight with you: the voice it calls you in is still Korean. That part I’m still working through — if it gets in your way, tell me and it moves up the list. |

 This is a work in progress. If something is awkward or broken, that's exactly what I want to hear.

title: Show HN: Rbit – Self Hosted Git Forge in Rust
author: GitRbit
body: rbit is a self hosted git forge designed around three core philosophies: speed, security, and efficiency.We built rbit using Rust, Axum, Askama, Gitoxide, SQLite + redb, HTMX + Tailwind. Every piece of the stack was carefully considered to provide users with the fastest possible experience working with their repos without sacrificing the functionality you've come to expect from your existing git forge.Our team is actively working to help make rbit the best it can be and we'd love to get your feedback while we continue improving!rbit is built using rbit and it's CI/CD pipeline, we are dogfooding as we build it in the open. It has been localized into 9 languages including: English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Russian, Chinese (Simplified), Japanese, and Korean. If you're a native speaker we would happily accept translation fixes!

Questions and answers.
Is Minute free? 
 Yes. Minute is free and open source, and it needs no account.
Does it work offline? 
 Yes. After you download the models once, Minute records, transcribes, summarizes, and answers questions with Wi-Fi turned off. It goes online only to download a model, to list models, and to check for an update. You can turn off the update check in Settings.
Does a bot join my Zoom or Teams call? 
 No. Minute records on your Mac. It captures your microphone and, on macOS 13 or later, the system audio, so it hears the other people on the call without joining it. Meeting detection covers Zoom, Teams, Webex, Slack, FaceTime, Discord, and calls in a browser, such as Google Meet.
Which Macs does it run on? 
 Minute needs macOS 11 or later. System audio needs macOS 13 or later and the Screen Recording permission. To notice that a call ended while the meeting app stays open, Minute needs macOS 14.2 or later. Apple silicon is the tested target. The Intel build is not yet tested on real Intel hardware, and the large Whisper models need Apple silicon. The smaller models need 8 GB of memory, the larger ones 16 GB.
Can it save notes to Obsidian? 
 Yes. Choose your vault folder in Settings, and Minute writes a Markdown file each time a summary finishes. It can add the date, title, duration, and speakers as properties. Without Obsidian, export any note as Markdown.
Is it open source?

title: Show HN: Strata Architecture
author: yrashk
body: I've long thought about how we're influenced by CPU architectures, and importantly, their ISAs.In a discussion at a meetup, I brought up a topic that interested me for a while: how would an ISA that exposes memory and cache interactions in a more explicit way (because if you think about it, memory is very much I/O), as opposed to being smart and predictive on its own?An obscure interest, of course. Nevertheless, I wanted to build a quick prototype after that.What ended up transpiring was a bit larger. A multicore architecture with tiered stores, capabilities, a JIT'd emulator, Verilog RTL with a simulator, a small microkernel OS, UI, JIT Forth, an assembler in its own assembly, a bootstrapping C99 compiler, a few games, a visual debugger, and a few other things.(This also shows just how far a directed LLM process can go in little time)

title: Show HN: Straum – PostgreSQL Group by in Microseconds
author: jeeybee
body:
I've seen too many slow-log queries with a GROUP BY that makes Postgres blow up, so for the last two weeks or so I've been working on Straum. You declare the aggregates as a view, and Straum answers over HTTP (other transports might be added). I've been using the New York taxi dataset as a benchmark. On the heavier GROUP BYs I see about 1,000x to 5,000x. It's written in Rust (of course).It leans on Postgres replication slots, logical or physical, to get its data. Postgres stays the source of truth.What do you think?Benchmark: https://janbjorge.github.io/straum/benchmark.html

title: Show HN: Perfectclone – Yoink the source code of any website, not an AI clone
author: eshaangulati
body:
# eshaangulati123/perfectclone

yoink any website. Clone any website 1:1 and get its real frontend files, not an AI-regenerated copy. Rebrand it, keep Next.js working, and deploy it as your own instantly

- Stars: 45
- Forks: 3
- Watchers: 45
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-11-04T03:13:53Z

## Languages

- Python

## Topics

- clone-website
- httrack-alternative
- nextjs
- playwright
- python
- static-site
- web-scraping
- website-cloner
- website-copier
- website-mirror

## Top Contributors

- eshaangulati123 (6 contributions)

---

## README

# perfectclone: website cloner that copies the real site, 1:1

**Pull the real frontend of any public site in ~15 seconds. No AI, no tokens.**

Clone any website. Get the real files. huly.io cloned with perfectclone: 0.00% pixel difference, 14 seconds, 157 files, 0 LLM calls.

perfectclone clones any website 1:1. It crawls the site with a real browser (Playwright),
downloads the site's own HTML, JavaScript, CSS, fonts and images, and gives you a folder you can
serve, edit and deploy. Then it lets you rebrand it, rehost it and strip the original owner's
trackers without breaking it, including Next.js sites that hydrate on load.

```bash
pip install perfectclone

perfectclone clone example.com
perfectclone serve example.com             # → http://localhost:8000
```

That's it. Chromium is downloaded automatically the first time you clone. Requires Python 3.10+.

Or try it without installing anything, using uv:

```bash
uvx perfectclone clone example.com
```

## Why not an AI cloner?

Most "clone any website" tools today regenerate the site: an AI agent looks at screenshots or
scraped markup, writes a new React/Next.js app, and compares the result against the original
with a visual-similarity score until it's close enough. That gets you a lookalike. The code is
new, the behaviour is approximate, and there are always gaps.

perfectclone doesn't regenerate anything. It mirrors the bytes the site actually serves, so
the clone *is* the site: same markup, same bundles, same animations, same JavaScript running.
Sometimes the real solution is the simple one.

| | AI cloners | wget / HTTrack | perfectclone |
| --------------------------------------- | :--------: | :------------: | :----------: |
| Copies the site's real files | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Pixel-identical on modern JS sites | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Catches lazy-loaded JS, fonts, images | — | ❌ | ✅ |
| React / Next.js sites still run | — | ❌ | ✅ |
| Rebrand without breaking the site | ✅ | ⚠️ | ✅ |
| Strips the original site's trackers | — | ❌ | ✅ |
| Works without an LLM or API key | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |

## Tested on real sites

Each card is one site split down the middle: the live site on the left, the clone on the right.

Live vs clone split view for nextjs.org, astro.build, svelte.dev, vitepress.dev, docusaurus.io and wordpress.org

`scripts/compat.py` clones each site, serves the copy, and compares its home page with the live
one at 1440×900, with animations and videos paused on the same frame:

| Site | Built with | Pixel match | Hydration errors | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| huly.io | Next.js | 100% | 0 | |
| nextjs.org | Next.js | 100% | 0 | |
| astro.build | Astro | 100% | 0 | |
| svelte.dev | SvelteKit | 100% | 0 | |
| vitepress.dev | VitePress (Vue) | 100% | 0 | |
| docusaurus.io | Docusaurus (React) | 100% | 0 | |
| wordpress.org/news | WordPress | 100% | 0 | |
| paulgraham.com | Hand-written HTML | 100% | 0 | |
| example.com | Static HTML | 100% | 0 | |
| framer.com | Framer | 96% | 0 | Cookie banner needs Framer's backend |
| webflow.com | Webflow | 93% | 0 | Cookie banner won't run on localhost; carousel caught mid-scroll |

Every clone loaded with zero requests to trackers. Run it yourself with
`python scripts/compat.py`, and please open an issue for any site that doesn't come out right.

## Commands

```bash
perfectclone clone <url> [-o out] [--max-pages 200] [--extract] [--keep-trackers] [--ignore-robots]
perfectclone serve <site> [-p 8000]
perfectclone replace <site> <old> <new> [--exact-case] [--substring]
perfectclone rehost <site> <old-origin> <new-origin>
perfectclone strip-trackers <site>
```

- **clone** writes `out/site/` (the working copy) and `out/manifest.json` (pages, failures,
 third-party hosts the site uses). `--extract` also saves each page's text, metadata
 (headings, links, images, forms, JSON-LD) and a full-page screenshot to `out/extract/`.
 Trackers are stripped by default.
- **replace** renames text everywhere: HTML, JS, CSS, JSON, SVG. It also handles the UPPER,
 lower and Capitalized variants, and leaves URLs and asset paths alone so nothing 404s.
- **rehost** points canonical, Open Graph, JSON-LD and sitemap URLs at your domain.
- **serve** works like a static host: clean URLs (`/about` → `/about/index.html`), and
 `/_next/image` requests are served from the mirrored originals.

Rebrand a clone and put it online:

```bash
perfectclone clone acme.com -o acme
perfectclone replace acme "Acme" "Globex"
perfectclone rehost  acme https://acme.com https://globex.com
npx netlify-cli deploy --dir acme/site --prod      # or any static host
```

## How it works

1. **Crawl with a real browser.** Each page is rendered in Chromium and scrolled to the bottom,
 and every response is recorded. That catches what static mirrors miss: code-split JS chunks,
 fonts requested from CSS, images behind lazy loading. Links are followed breadth-first,
 seeded from the sitemap. robots.txt is respected unless you pass `--ignore-robots`.
2. **Mirror the server's bytes.** Pages are saved as the HTML the *server* sends, not the
 rendered DOM, because that's what the site's JavaScript expects to hydrate. Assets keep
 their URL paths, and CSS/JS are scanned for further references (`url()`, `srcset`, chunk
 paths) until nothing new turns up.
3. **Edit without breaking hydration.** A Next.js App Router page ships its HTML *and* a
 serialized copy of the React tree in `self.__next_f.push(...)` script chunks. Change one and
 not the other, and React throws a hydration error and re-renders from the payload, undoing
 your edit. perfectclone decodes the payload stream, edits it row by row, recomputes the
 UTF-8 byte lengths of length-prefixed text rows (`:T,…`), rejoins rows that span
 chunks, and writes it back next to the matching HTML edit.
4. **Strip trackers.** Google Analytics/Tag Manager, the Meta pixel, LinkedIn Insight, Hotjar,
 Clarity, Segment, PostHog, HubSpot, TikTok, Reddit, X, Cloudflare Web Analytics, RB2B and
 more. They're removed from ` `/` ` tags, from preload hints, and from Next.js
 `next/script` elements that only exist in the payload.

## Limits

- **No backend.** Forms, logins, search and API calls still go to the original servers (or
 fail). perfectclone copies the front end.
- **Next.js client-side navigation** needs each page's RSC payload answered for `?_rsc=`
 requests. perfectclone mirrors them and `perfectclone serve` routes them. On a plain static
 host, internal links fall back to full page loads: everything still works, just without the
 instant transitions.
- **Chunks that are only requested after a click** (say, a modal's code) are captured if the
 crawl triggered them or a bundle names them as a string. A bundle can also assemble a chunk
 URL at runtime, and that one may be missed.
- **Bot protection** (CAPTCHAs, aggressive Cloudflare rules) can block the crawl. perfectclone
 does not try to get around it.
- Embeds (YouTube, Cal.com, maps) and third-party CDNs keep loading from their own hosts.

## Roadmap

**Clone apps behind a login, like dashboards.** Today perfectclone sees what an anonymous visitor
sees, and data that loads from APIs after the page renders isn't kept. The plan, for apps you
have an account on:

- **Crawl as you.** Sign in once in a browser window; perfectclone saves the session and
 crawls with it.
- **Record API responses.** Keep every JSON response the app fetches during the crawl and have
 `perfectclone serve` replay them, so charts, tables and lists show real data offline.
- **Explore by clicking.** Click through navigation, tabs and menus to reach views that only
 exist in client-side routing.

The result is a clickable snapshot of the UI and its data at capture time. Saving, server-side
filtering and live updates still need the real backend.

Other ideas: hydration-aware editing for Nuxt, SvelteKit and Remix payloads, and a deploy
helper that writes `_redirects` / `vercel.json` rules so `?_rsc=` and `/_next/image` work on
static hosts. Contributions welcome.

## Contributing

perfectclone is open source under the MIT License. Issues and pull requests are
welcome, especially reports of sites that don't clone cleanly. See
CONTRIBUTING.md, and please follow the Code of Conduct.
Report security issues privately as described in SECURITY.md.

## README

# arm64-recompiler

A static recompiler that turns real Windows x86-64 PE binaries into native Apple Silicon (ARM64) Mach-O executables. It lifts the original machine code to LLVM IR ahead of time and compiles that IR for macOS; there is no instruction-level emulation of the lifted code at run time.

## What works today

- **PuTTY Plink 0.83, natively.** The original Windows release runs `-V` through full CRT startup, argument parsing, standard output and shutdown. Output matches the original binary under Wine + Rosetta byte-for-byte, at **6.20× the speed** (42.31 ms vs. 262.23 ms) and with a **68.9% smaller memory footprint** (5.51 MB vs. 17.74 MB RSS).
- **PuTTY 0.83 GUI.** The original Windows release renders its configuration dialog and opens raw and **SSH** terminal sessions (hybrid NTRU Prime / Curve25519 key exchange, Ed25519 public-key login, AES-256).
- **Plink over SSH.** Key exchange, public-key login, a remote command and exit status 0 against OpenSSH.
- **jq 1.8.2.** Runs real workloads; verified against the upstream macOS build for stdin, file input, Unicode filenames, sorting, regex and error handling.
- **ripgrep 14.1.1.** Completes a single-threaded recursive search with matches and exit status agreeing with Wine.
- **Runtime DLL loading.** `LoadLibrary`, named exports, callbacks, thread-local storage and unload, on the main thread and on a worker thread. Wine's own `ntdll`, `kernelbase`, `ucrtbase`, `user32`, `gdi32`, `comctl32` and `ws2_32` are lifted as ordinary guest DLLs.

## Current limitations

This is not a general "run any Windows binary" tool.

- **GUI and network programs need hosted mode.** The program and Wine's Windows-side DLLs are lifted to ARM64, but Wine's unix-side syscall layer, a Wine 11.0 install and a Wine prefix are still required, and Wine's `wineserver` runs under Rosetta. There is no standalone `.app` bundle.
- **Coverage is driven by the programs tried so far.** AES-NI, SHA extensions, carry-less multiply and AVX are not lifted. PuTTY and Plink are built with `--trace`, which accepts untranslated code and traps if execution reaches it; they avoid those paths because the reported CPU features select their software ciphers.
- **Some code still runs in a fallback x86 interpreter**: runtime-generated code, and code reached through indirect jumps the lifter did not recover.
- **Hosted programs use more memory.** The lifted PuTTY GUI opens slightly sooner than under Wine + Rosetta and an SSH command runs level or faster, but memory use is 1.6 to 2 times higher. See Performance.
- **ripgrep runs only single-threaded, through the launcher in diagnostic mode.**
- Direct3D is not started.

## War stories

Static recompilation from Windows x86-64 to Apple Silicon is full of edge cases and undocumented runtime behavior. **`WAR_STORIES.md`** is a detailed account of the failures and how each was resolved:

1. **The Indirect Branch & Callback Discovery Trap**: how PE `.pdata` exception directory parsing replaced multi-pass discovery.
2. **The `lock cmpxchg` Flag Calculation Bug**: an inverted operand in x86 `CMP` flag emulation broke atomic spinlocks.
3. **The TLS Callback Chicken-and-Egg Trap**: why `jq` and `rg` crashed before `AddressOfEntryPoint` without pre-main TLS callbacks.
4. **The Universal Import Filter Blocker**: hardcoding `KERNEL32.dll` silently dropped Universal CRT functions.
5. **The Modern Windows API-Set Prefix Maze**: schema-based virtual DLL indirection in MSVC and Rust binaries.
6. **The UCRT `_iobuf` / `FILE*` Memory Impasse**: why fake stream handles crash guest code and how bounded `_iobuf` tables fixed it.
7. **Virtual Memory Protection Translation**: mapping Win32 page protection bitmasks to POSIX `mprotect`.
8. **The Pointer That Was Not Equal to Itself**: PuTTY's key exchange asserted because stored pointers were image-relative and computed ones were not.
9. **The Function That Returned Halfway Through**: MSVC's chained unwind ranges, and a jump the lifter emitted as a return.
10. **Critical Sections That Were Not Locks**: the single-threaded shortcut that Plink's input thread broke.
11. **The Build Machine That Deleted the Source**: iCloud evicting source files and built libraries mid-session.

## Performance

### Plink `-V` (native)

Measured on Apple Silicon across 30 runs per variant (after 2 warmups) with an optimized static ARM64 Mach-O:

| Variant | Min / Median / P95 Latency | Speedup vs. Wine | Peak RSS |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Recompiled Native ARM64 (`-O2`)** | **41.72 / 42.31 / 44.04 ms** | **6.20×** | **5.51 MB** |
| Original Windows binary (Wine + Rosetta) | 248.24 / 262.23 / 383.70 ms | 1.00× | 17.74 MB |
| Upstream macOS ARM64 build | 6.87 / 7.41 / 7.98 ms | 35.39× | 2.23 MB |

Both the recompiled ARM64 executable and Wine + Rosetta matched stdout byte-for-byte and exited with status 0.

### Hosted programs (PuTTY GUI and Plink over SSH)

Measured on an Apple M1, five runs per variant after one warm-up, with other work running on the machine. "Cold" runs start from a stopped `wineserver`, so its start-up is included in both columns; "warm" runs find it already running. Memory is the resident size of the program's own process.

| Measurement | Lifted ARM64 (hosted) | Original under Wine + Rosetta | Ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| PuTTY: launch to configuration window, cold (min / median / max) | **1798 / 1932 / 1989 ms** | 2116 / 2148 / 2293 ms | 1.11× faster |
| PuTTY: resident memory with the dialog open | 125 MB | 63 MB | 2.0× more |
| Plink: SSH login, `echo`, exit, cold (min / median / max) | 1692 / 1839 / 2220 ms | 1735 / 1802 / 1847 ms | 0.98× (about equal) |
| Plink: SSH login, `echo`, exit, warm (min / median / max) | **284 / 293 / 296 ms** | 389 / 452 / 583 ms | 1.54× faster |
| Plink: peak resident memory | 36.5 MB | 22.7 MB | 1.6× more |

Cold starts are dominated by `wineserver` start-up, which both variants pay, so the lifted programs are only slightly ahead or level there. With the server running, the lifted SSH command is about one and a half times as fast. Memory use is 1.6 to 2 times higher; that has not been investigated yet. The program's own code is compiled at `-O2` (set `ARM64_RECOMPILER_PROGRAM_OPT` to change it), and `--trace` costs one store per guest instruction.

## Quickstart

From the repository root on an Apple Silicon Mac with Clang and Python. To set up the Python environment:

```sh
python3 -m venv work/venv
work/venv/bin/python3 -m pip install -r recompiler/requirements.txt
```

### 1. Run the regression test suite

Exercises 11,121 arithmetic and control-flow instruction permutations, atomic `lock cmpxchg`, data relocations, and console tests:

```sh
PYTHON="$PWD/work/venv/bin/python3" recompiler/run.sh
```

It also runs the virtual-memory test (`test_mmap.c`) and seven fixtures:
- `recompiler/fixtures/vm_fault`: raw `VirtualAlloc` faults reach VEH and table-driven SEH handlers, including a resumption in the middle of a function.
- `recompiler/fixtures/jit`: runtime-generated code in `PAGE_EXECUTE*` buffers runs in the fallback x86 interpreter, plus RWX patching and DEP faults.
- `recompiler/fixtures/exception/test_msvc.sh`: MSVC C++ EH and `__try`/`__except`.
- `recompiler/fixtures/ntdll`: Wine's x64 `ntdll.dll` and `kernelbase.dll` are lifted as guest modules when they are shipped beside the program. Wine's own `Rtl*`, path, string and locale code runs as lifted code, including kernelbase's real `DllMain`. ntdll exports that own process-wide state stay in the runtime, so heaps, last error, locks, TLS/FLS, the loader and exceptions are shared with the runtime's kernel32. Those exports are the syscall stubs plus the list in `NTDLL_RUNTIME_EXPORTS` in `recompiler/build_console_modules.py`. Unimplemented syscalls return `STATUS_NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. When kernelbase.dll is shipped, a kernel32 (or other system) function with no runtime shim falls back to kernelbase's lifted export of the same name. The runtime also installs ntdll's code-page and case tables, the startup step Wine's own loader normally performs. kernelbase reads Wine's NLS tables from `ARM64_RECOMPILER_NLS_DIR`, which the fixture sets to Wine's `share/wine/nls`.
- `recompiler/fixtures/gui`: a Win32 program registers a class, opens a window and paints it through lifted `user32.dll` and `gdi32.dll`, with the syscalls served natively by `win32u.so` and `winemac.so`. Needs the hosted-mode build (`recompiler/wine-host/build.sh`) and a logged-in GUI session; otherwise it prints `SKIP`.
- `recompiler/fixtures/winsock`: a TCP client connects to a local echo server, sends, waits with `select` and receives, through lifted `ws2_32.dll` and the native socket layer. Needs the hosted-mode build.
- `recompiler/fixtures/crt`: Wine's real x64 `ucrtbase.dll` is lifted and loaded in place of the runtime's CRT shims. This covers API sets, ordinal imports, forwarded exports, and `DllMain` attach/detach order. It needs the same SDK tools as the MSVC case, plus a `ucrtbase.dll` from Wine.

The fixtures compare against Wine when it is installed (`recompiler/setup_wine.py`, or `WINE`/`WINEPREFIX`). The MSVC case needs an xwin SDK (`XWIN_SDK`) and LLVM `clang-cl`/`lld-link`. Without them it prints `SKIP`, or fails if `REQUIRE_MSVC=1`.

### 2. Reproduce the Plink milestone

Recompiles the original `plink.exe` and verifies `-V` output and exit status:

```sh
PYTHON="$PWD/work/venv/bin/python3" \
  recompiler/test_plink_startup.sh "$PWD/work/corpus/plink.exe"
```

With automatic `.pdata` function discovery, this succeeds on **attempt 0**, printing `plink: Release 0.83` and exiting with status 0.

### 3. Build and verify jq 1.8.2

Needs a matching LLVM 22 Clang and `llvm-link`. Set `LLVM_BIN` to their bin directory if LLVM is installed outside `/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm@22/bin`. The parity test takes the macOS ARM64 jq 1.8.2 release as its reference.

```sh
PYTHON="$PWD/work/venv/bin/python3" \
  recompiler/build_jq.sh work/corpus/jq.exe work/build/jq-arm64
curl -fsSL https://github.com/jqlang/jq/releases/download/jq-1.8.2/jq-macos-arm64 \
  -o work/build/jq-reference
chmod +x work/build/jq-reference
work/venv/bin/python3 recompiler/test_jq.py work/build/jq-arm64 work/build/jq-reference
```

The test checks stdout, stderr, and exit codes for stdin, file input, Unicode filenames, sorting, regex, malformed JSON, and jq's `-e` behavior.

### 4. Verify runtime DLL loading

The fixture builds a Windows EXE and DLL, recompiles them to ARM64, and checks runtime loading, named exports, callbacks, thread-local storage, and unload on the main thread and on a worker thread:

```sh
PYTHON="$PWD/work/venv/bin/python3" \
  recompiler/fixtures/dynamic_dll/test.sh
```

### 5. Trace startup of corpus binaries

Trace native execution and inspect the stopping point for other Windows binaries:

```sh
# jq 1.8.2
$PWD/work/venv/bin/python3 recompiler/trace_callbacks.py --max-attempts 1 work/corpus/jq.exe --version

# ripgrep 14.1.1
$PWD/work/venv/bin/python3 recompiler/run_exe.py --trace work/corpus/rg.exe --threads 1 --no-config --no-heading --sort path -n PATTERN DIRECTORY
```

### 6. Run a Windows GUI or network program (hosted mode)

Hosted mode needs an x86-64 Wine 11.0 install (`setup_wine.py` puts one under `work/wine`) and Wine's unix side built natively for arm64. Build that once (needs Xcode's clang, Homebrew LLVM, FreeType and `bison` 3 or newer):

```sh
recompiler/wine-host/build.sh "$PWD/work/wine-host"
```

Then `lift_app.py` lifts a program together with the Wine DLLs it needs and can start it. It follows static imports, export forwarders, and delay imports one level deep:

```sh
# Wine's Task Manager: tab control, list views, status bar, worker threads.
work/venv/bin/python3 recompiler/wine-host/lift_app.py \
  "work/wine/Wine Stable.app/Contents/Resources/wine/lib/wine/x86_64-windows/taskmgr.exe" \
  work/build/taskmgr --run

# PuTTY 0.83 GUI (download putty.exe from the PuTTY site and check its SHA-256 first).
work/venv/bin/python3 recompiler/wine-host/lift_app.py \
  work/corpus/putty-0.83/putty.exe work/build/putty \
  --dll ws2_32.dll --dll comctl32.dll --trace --run
```

- `--dll NAME` also lifts a Wine DLL the program loads with `LoadLibrary`.
- `--delay-depth N` sets how many levels of delay imports to follow (default 1).
- `--trace` accepts program code the lifter cannot translate yet. That code traps, reporting its address, only if execution reaches it. PuTTY needs this for its AES-NI and SHA paths, which it does not take because the reported CPU features select its software ciphers.
- `--run [ARGS]` starts the lifted program with the hosted environment.

The first build of each DLL is slow (a few minutes for PuTTY's 48 DLLs); later builds reuse them and take seconds.

### 7. Shared lifted modules

A lifted DLL is built once as its own shared library and reused by every program, instead of being linked into each one. A relocated DLL loads at an address derived from its file name, so the same library fits any program.

- The store is `~/Library/Caches/arm64-recompiler/modules`; set `ARM64_RECOMPILER_MODULE_STORE` to move it.
- At startup the runtime looks for each library in `ARM64_RECOMPILER_MODULE_DIR`, beside the program, in `../Frameworks`, then in the store.
- `ARM64_RECOMPILER_STATIC_MODULES=1` or `ARM64_RECOMPILER_NO_CACHE=1` links the DLLs into the program instead.
- The program's own lifted code is compiled at `-O2` and its object is kept in the same store, keyed by the lifted IR, so only the first build of a program pays for it (about a minute for Plink). `ARM64_RECOMPILER_PROGRAM_OPT=-O0` trades run time for build time.
- Programs lifted with `--trace` record the current guest address with one store per instruction. The runtime's `GUEST_WATCH_RVA` and `ARM64_RECOMPILER_PC_LOG` debugging aids need a call per instruction instead: lift with `ARM64_RECOMPILER_TRACE_HOOKS=1` to use them.
- A library is rebuilt when the DLL or the lifter changes, but not when only `console_runtime.c` changes. After a runtime change that alters what lifted code expects, clear the store.

With shared modules the GUI fixture's binary is under 1 MB instead of 40 MB.

## How it works

### Whole-program lifter (`console_lift.py`)

- **PE decoding and IR generation**: uses Capstone to decode x86-64 instructions into LLVM IR functions that share one register and flag context across guest calls.
- **Automatic `.pdata` function discovery**: parses the PE Exception Directory (`IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXCEPTION` / `RUNTIME_FUNCTION` entries) to register valid function entry RVAs in the runtime indirect-call dispatch table.
- **Atomics**: `lock cmpxchg` (32-bit and 64-bit `r/m, reg`) is lowered to LLVM atomic `cmpxchg seq_cst` with exact x86 `CMP` flag emulation (`ZF`, `CF`, `SF`, `OF`).
- **Cross-DLL import resolution**: resolves imports across multiple DLLs (`KERNEL32.dll`, `api-ms-win-crt-*`, etc.), mapping them to runtime implementations or dispatch stubs.
- **Call and return integrity**: simulates the x86 stack return slot and validates the return target before executing a return.

### Runtime environment (`console_runtime.c`)

- **TLS and callbacks**: parses PE `IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_TLS` and executes TLS callback routines (`DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH`) before the program entry point.
- **Fiber Local Storage (FLS)**: `FlsAlloc`, `FlsFree`, `FlsGetValue`, `FlsSetValue`, and `FlsGetValue2`.
- **Memory and protection**: bounded guest sections, heap (`HeapAlloc`, `HeapReAlloc`, `HeapFree`), and `VirtualProtect` (mapping Win32 page protections to POSIX `mprotect`).
- **Synchronization**: critical sections (`InitializeCriticalSection`, `InitializeCriticalSectionAndSpinCount`, `EnterCriticalSection`, `TryEnterCriticalSection`, `LeaveCriticalSection`, `DeleteCriticalSection`) are real locks: the owner is claimed with a compare-and-swap and contended threads wait.
- **Dynamic API sets**: prefix-based routing in `LoadLibraryExW` / `GetModuleHandleW` for `api-ms-win-core-*` (fibers, synch, localization, datetime, processthreads, sysinfo).
- **UCRT stdio**: `__acrt_iob_func` with standard stream `_iobuf` structures (`stdin`, `stdout`, `stderr`), `_errno`, `fwrite`, `fputs`, `fflush`, `fputc`, `putchar`, and `puts`.
- **Environment and process setup**: `GetCommandLineW`, `CommandLineToArgvW`, `GetEnvironmentStringsW`, `GetModuleHandleW`, and `GetProcAddress`.

### Hosted mode (`wine-host/`)

For GUI and network programs, the program and Wine's x86-64 Windows DLLs (`user32`, `gdi32`, `comctl32`, `ws2_32`, and the rest) are lifted to ARM64. Only the syscall layer (`ntdll.so`, `win32u.so`, `winemac.so`, `ws2_32.so`) is Wine's native code, built for arm64 with a small host-mode patch.

## Corpus status

| Binary | Status | Current frontier / stopping point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`plink.exe`** (0.83) | **Fully functional (`-V`)** | Prints `plink: Release 0.83` and exits 0 on attempt 0. |
| **`plink.exe`** (0.83), hosted | **SSH command over the network** | Key exchange, public-key login, remote command and exit status 0 against OpenSSH, through lifted `ws2_32.dll`. |
| **`putty.exe`** (0.83), hosted | **GUI runs: configuration dialog, raw and SSH sessions** | Not in the repository; see hosted mode above. Hardware-accelerated crypto paths are not lifted. |
| **`taskmgr.exe`** (Wine 11.0), hosted | **GUI runs** | Tabs, list views and a live status bar on lifted `comctl32.dll`. |
| **`gui_showcase.exe`** | **Fully functional (hybrid GUI)** | Executes Win32 `MessageBoxA` natively on macOS, displaying the alert and exiting 0. |
| **`jq.exe`** (1.8.2) | Runs real jq workloads | Verified for stdin, file input, sorting, regex, and error handling. See the jq parity test above. |
| **`rg.exe`** (14.1.1) | Completes a single-threaded recursive search via the launcher in diagnostic mode | Both expected matches and exit status agree with Wine using `--no-heading --sort path`. |

## Roadmap: hybrid native AOT + GUI thunking

The long-term goal is to go beyond console utilities and run complex Windows software at native Apple Silicon speed without reimplementing decades of Windows display infrastructure.

### Status

The GUI half of this plan now exists as hosted mode. It goes one step further than thunking into Wine: Wine's Windows-side DLLs are lifted along with the program, and only Wine's unix-side syscall layer runs as native code. Current limits:

- Wine's `wineserver` and its helper processes are still the x86-64 install's own, so they run under Rosetta, and a Wine prefix is required. There is no standalone `.app` bundle yet.
- Every linked DLL is loaded at startup, used or not. That costs little time (tens of milliseconds for Plink's 14), but lifted programs use 1.6 to 2 times the memory of the original under Wine.
- `DLL_THREAD_ATTACH` is not delivered to threads Wine creates.
- Instruction coverage is still driven by the programs tried so far: AES-NI, SHA, carry-less multiply and AVX are not lifted.
- Direct3D and the "Metal thunking" part of the diagram are not started.

### The hybrid architecture

Rather than writing a replacement for the Windows GUI subsystems (USER32, GDI, Direct3D, Direct2D, COM, WinUI), the plan is a hybrid of ahead-of-time recompilation and API thunking:

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│             Windows x86-64 PE Application             │
└──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                           │
             [Static LLVM IR Recompiler]
                           │
                           ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           Native Apple Silicon ARM64 Mach-O            │
│  • Application Business Logic & Math (Full AOT Speed)   │
│  • Memory Management & Heap Allocator (Native macOS)   │
│  • Multi-threading & Atomics (Native Hardware CAS)     │
└────────────┬───────────────────────────────┬───────────┘
             │                               │
    [System & File I/O]             [GUI & Graphics Calls]
             │                               │
             ▼                               ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐     ┌────────────────────────┐
│   Native POSIX Shims    │     │   Wine / Rosetta /     │
│   (Console, FS, Net)    │     │   Metal Thunking Layer │
└─────────────────────────┘     │ (USER32, GDI, Direct3D)│
                                └────────────────────────┘
```

### Why this architecture

- **CPU work runs as native code.** Parsing, arithmetic and inner loops are compiled ahead of time for Apple Silicon.
- **Windowing reuses Wine.** Wine has more than 30 years of work on USER32/GDI message loops, font rasterization and display drivers on macOS. Calling into it, or bridging Direct3D to Metal as Apple's Game Porting Toolkit and DXMT do, avoids rebuilding that surface.

## Repository layout

| Path | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `recompiler/` | Core lifters, runtime emulation, diagnostics, and test harness |
| `recompiler/console_lift.py` | Whole-program PE x86-64 lifter emitting LLVM IR |
| `recompiler/console_runtime.c` | Minimal Win32 / CRT runtime shim (memory, TEB/PEB, TLS, FLS, sync, stdio) |
| `recompiler/build_console_modules.py` | Builds a program with its lifted DLLs; owns the shared module store |
| `recompiler/wine-host/` | Hosted mode: Wine 11.0 unix-side build, host-mode patch, syscall thunks, and `lift_app.py` |
| `recompiler/fixtures/` | End-to-end fixtures (faults, JIT, exceptions, ntdll, CRT, GUI, Winsock, DLL loading) |
| `WAR_STORIES.md` | Post-mortem of failures, subtle bugs, and how they were fixed |
| `work/corpus/` | Original Windows x64 release binaries (`plink.exe`, `jq.exe`, `rg.exe`) |
| `work/` | Test environments, diagnostic traces, and generated builds |

title: Show HN: Widefleet Cloud - Deploy agent-built internal apps with SSO and storage
author: jonathan_laib
body:
Hi HN, we’re building Widefleet for teams building internal apps and workflows with coding agents.Think Vercel or Cloudflare, with company login (SSO), app sharing, and controls for IT to manage who can access each app and which company systems it can connect to. Apps run as separate workers with per-app databases and object storage. You can also fully customize and manage connectors to internal systems, so your other users don’t have to handle API keys etc. themselves. Cron jobs and queues support background tasks and recurring workflows.There’s now a hosted version, so give it a try and let us know what you think!Try it: https://app.widefleet.com
Code: https://github.com/widefleet/widefleetCurious how you’re dealing with vibe-coded apps at work, whether you built them yourself or ended up maintaining someone else’s.

title: Show HN: Bad Apple but it's Strava [video]
author: kevinlinxc
body:
Hi HN!Here to show off a project that took 18 months, 7KLOC, and more importantly, 194 kilometres of walking! In a nutshell, I wanted to make the famous silhouette animation “Bad Apple” with Strava, which is an exercise tracking app that visualizes where you walk/run on a map. To use the earth as my canvas, I had to do a lot of coding in the prep work to plan where I would walk for each frame of the animation. As I explain in the video, my problem solving/coding steps were something like this:- split video into frames, determine a good framerate- detect contours with OpenCV for each frame. Since frames are very diverse, I had to start with some heuristics for choosing contours and ultimately make a GUI to manually curate all 438 of them (e.g. some frames had many small contours while others had a few important ones, and the video is constantly inverting colours). Output of this work was an intermediate json list of x,y coordinates representing the path along contours- convert these cartesian coordinates into the Universal Transverse Mercator coordinate system, which represents the earth in a cartesian system (as opposed to GPS which doesn’t lend to adding relative distances in degrees very well)- convert UTM to GPS using a package, then to the GPX file format which is universally accepted- Import GPX files into an app that shows where I am and where I need to walk (I used Gaia GPS). Then I turned on Strava in the background and walked for ~18 months until this was done.I also had to make a bunch of custom software to visualize these walks and make montages of them, like a script to pull polylines from the Strava API, a custom polyline renderer, a script to censor my strava activities a bit, and much more. title: Show HN: Learn Piano Easy App – Free and Open Source
author: AnotherBrainFoo
body:
Learn Piano Easy

# Learn Piano Easy

Watch the notes fall onto the keys, then play them yourself, one song at a time.

- No account
- Works offline
- No ads

Hi, I'm your piano teacher. Shall we play?

## The notes fall, and you play

Every song looks like this. Each note falls onto its key, and you press the key as it lands.

Once it plays, press its keys to join in.

## Learn step by step, or just play

Pick the part that fits your day. You can switch at any time.

Guided course

### Learn Piano

A guided course of small steps. Each one teaches a skill, and a song puts it to use.

Any song

### Just Play Piano

Open any song, watch its notes fly towards a 3D piano, and play along.

## Four steps, again and again

Every lesson follows the same short loop, so you always know what comes next.

1. 1

### Learn a skill

A short lesson shows one new thing, such as a note, a rhythm or a hand position.
2. 2

### Practise it

Play it on your own keyboard. The piano waits for you and marks each right note.
3. 3

### Play a real song

Use the skill in a song from the library, at a level that fits you.
4. 4

### Earn badges

Each lesson earns XP, and each world you finish earns a badge.

## Every song grows with you

Each song of ours comes in four versions. Switch between them and watch Ode to Joy grow.

Beginner Easy Medium Hard

Your first days. One hand position, slow notes and a bass that waits for you.

## No piano? Start anyway

Any of these plays the notes. A real keyboard feels best, and the others let you start today.

- ### A MIDI keyboard

Plug it in by USB and allow MIDI once. From then on, the site finds it by itself.
- ### A touch screen

Tap the keys on the screen, with as many fingers as you like.
- ### Your computer keyboard

The letter and number keys play two octaves, and you can move any note to another key.

Touch a key to hear it.

## Nothing to pay, nothing to sign

The site is a gift from someone who loves the piano. It stays free.

- ### Free, with no account

Open the site and play. There is no sign-up and nothing to buy.
- ### Open source

Every line of code is public under the MIT License. Read it, change it, share it.
- ### Works offline

Once loaded, the site runs without a network. Songs you have opened play offline too.
- ### No ads, no profiles

Nothing you play leaves your device. We only count page visits, without cookies, and sell nothing.

## What people ask first

Do I need a piano?

No. A MIDI keyboard is best, but a touch screen or your computer keyboard plays every note too.

Which browsers work?

Any current browser plays. A MIDI keyboard needs Web MIDI, which Chrome, Edge and Firefox have and Safari lacks.

Do I need an account?

No. There is nothing to sign up for, and your settings stay in this browser.

Does it work offline?

Yes. Open the site once while online, and it runs offline from then on. A song plays offline once you have opened it.

Can I play my own songs?

Yes. Open any MIDI or MusicXML file in Just Play Piano. It is read on your device and never uploaded.

Which songs are in the library?

Our own arrangements of well-known tunes, each in four versions, a few pieces of our own, and classical pieces from open collections.

Is it really free?

Yes. It is open source under the MIT License, with no ads and no paid tier.

## Ready when you are

Pick a way in. You can switch at any time.

title: Show HN: Attest – Test what AI agents do, not just what they say
author: tommathews
body:
Skip to content Attest Framework 
 Search Ctrl K Cancel 
GitHub 
 Overview 
 Python SDK 
 TypeScript SDK 
 Guides 
 Architecture 
 Reference 
 Migration 
 Changelog 
Attest
 Test what your AI agent says, does and changes. Replay recorded model responses. Check the results before merging.
Get Started (Python) Get Started (TypeScript) Run the demo (refund-desk) 
Attest 1.1.0 is a testing framework for AI agents in Python and TypeScript. Check a reply, a sequence of tool calls or a change to external state with pytest or Vitest. Start with deterministic checks; add a model judge only for criteria those checks cannot express.
rec → replay → gate
 Section titled “rec → replay → gate” 
A support agent refunded a customer twice after a payment timeout. Its output-only tests stayed green. That synthetic incident — INC-1042 — becomes a regression test in three moves:
● rec Capture the incident
 attest capture records the trace and model exchanges, applies redaction and drafts contracts from the run. A fixture marked consistent with the recording is not proof that the behavior is correct: review the fixture and choose independent business invariants.
▶ replay Replay in CI
 Strict replay runs your agent’s real code against recorded model responses through a local proxy, with zero live model calls for matching requests. It removes live-model variability, not other sources of flaky tests; tool dependencies and test isolation still need control.
✓ gate Gate the merge
 Checks report pass , fail or not_evaluated with a reason. Failed tests block by default ( tests_failed: block ); not_evaluated warns unless the policy sets not_evaluated: block . Require the policy check in branch protection. The gate covers the contracts and baselines you supply, not every possible regression.
The tour follows the double-refund ledger, reviewed contracts, a blocked revert PR, mutation scores and the HTML viewer. Its outputs illustrate the synthetic demo; the demo README has the current executable walkthrough.
expect ( trace ). tool_cardinality ( " issue_refund " , per = " order_id " , at_most = 1 ) 
attestExpect (trace) . toolCardinality ( " issue_refund " , { per: " order_id " , atMost: 1 }); 
One line of behavior contract states the rule INC-1042 broke — over the trace’s tool calls, not the reply text.
Six evaluated layers plus plugins
 Section titled “Six evaluated layers plus plugins” 
The replay and gate run on deterministic checks. The layers are the full ladder of checks a contract or test can use, from free and instant to LLM-judged. Plugins add your own assertions. The table is generated from attest-engine capabilities --json .
1 Schema validation
 Checks the output against a JSON Schema.
Free 
 2 Constraint checks
 Checks cost, token, latency and step-count limits.
Free 
 3 Trace and behavioral checks
 Checks which tools ran, in which order, with which arguments, how often per business key, across the agent tree and against the world's final state.
Free 
 4 Content pattern matching
 Checks the output text against substrings, patterns and keywords.
Free 
 5 Embedding similarity
 Scores semantic similarity against a reference with an embedding model: OpenAI embeddings are paid, the local ONNX model is free.
Depends on provider 
 6 LLM-as-judge
 Scores the output against a rubric with a judge model: OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini judges are paid, a local ACP agent or an OpenAI-compatible local endpoint is not.
Depends on provider 
 + Plugins
 Custom assertions that run in the SDK process; cost and determinism are the plugin's.
Defined by the plugin 
What it looks like
 Section titled “What it looks like” 
Python
 Section titled “Python” 
from attest import agent, expect 
@agent ( " weather-agent " ) 
def weather_agent ( builder , query : str ) -> dict : 
# Recorded sample data: no model or weather API is called. 
builder. add_tool_call ( 
" get_weather " , 
args = { " city " : " Tokyo " } , 
result = { " temperature_c " : 22 , " conditions " : " Sunny " } , 
) 
return { 
" message " : " Current weather conditions in Tokyo: sunny, 22°C. " , 
" structured " : { " city " : " Tokyo " , " temperature_c " : 22 }, 
} 
def test_weather_agent ( attest ) : 
result = weather_agent ( query = " What's the weather in Tokyo? " ) 
chain = ( 
expect ( result ) 
. required_tools ( [ " get_weather " ] ) # L3, free 
. output_contains ( " Tokyo " ) # L4, free 
. output_matches_schema ( { # L1, free 
" type " : " object " , 
" required " : [ " city " , " temperature_c " ] , 
" properties " : { 
" city " : { " type " : " string " }, 
" temperature_c " : { " type " : " number " }, 
}, 
} ) 
) 
attest. evaluate ( chain )

TypeScript

} ); 
test ( ' weather agent returns weather data ' , async () => { 
const result = weatherAgent ( { query: ' What is the weather in Tokyo? ' } ); 
const chain = attestExpect (result) 
. requiredTools ([ ' get_weather ' ]) // Layer 3: Free 
. outputContains ( ' Tokyo ' ) // Layer 4: Free 
. outputNotContains ( ' error ' ); // Layer 4: Free 
await evaluate (chain); 
});

Save as weather.test.ts and install with npm install -D "@attest-ai/core@>=1.1.0" "@attest-ai/vitest@>=1.1.0" "vitest@^4" . Run npx attest doctor once to download and check the engine before npx vitest run : a cold first download can exceed Vitest’s default timeout. This test makes no provider calls.
Features
 Section titled “Features” 
Framework Adapters 
 Provider and framework adapters for Python and TypeScript, each with a maturity tier - the table below lists them.
Multi-Agent Testing 
 Beta: trace delegation chains and check parent-child relationships, ordering and cross-agent data flow.
Simulation Mode 
 Beta: use mock tools, seeded faults and user personas. Your application’s own network calls still need mocks or replay.
Continuous Evaluation 
 Experimental: sample application traces and alert on hard failures or score drift through Slack or webhooks.
Stable workflows include capture , strict replay , behavior contracts , world effects and CI policies and baselines . The overview links every feature and its maturity tier.

 experimental : Shipped without a stability commitment and without demonstrated demand; it can change or be removed in any release.

title: Show HN: Fondue – A meeting where everyone talks at once
author: blu3mo

Pause AI for five years? - Fondue

## Goal for this session

A public Fondue demo for Hacker News readers, on one question: if you could pause AI development worldwide for five years, would you?

So far two people would probably pause and one probably wouldn't. Four arguments are open below, and yours could tip one or open a new one.

- In Fondue, everyone talks with their own AI at the same time, and another AI brings those conversations together on one board like this.
- Bluemo built Fondue for small team meetings and opened this board to try it with Hacker News readers.
- To join, talk through your answer with the AI for a few minutes. What you say lands under the argument it bears on, and each line links to the words it came from.
- Rashik, who works at a frontier AI lab, and Maya, a high school teacher, would probably pause. Bluemo probably wouldn't. Rashik's question to Bluemo, and to everyone who wouldn't pause, is still unanswered.

## 1. If we build AI much smarter than us, could we keep control of it?

Rashik would pause for this reason, and says it is the mainstream reason the board was missing. He honestly doesn't know whether we could keep control, and he doesn't think we should wait for proof that something will go wrong. The pull the other way is medical research: better AI might help develop treatments for diseases we can't cure today.

Still open: for those who wouldn't pause, is losing control unlikely, or are the benefits worth the risk?

- R I would press the button, assuming it really stops development everywhere and we can still use the models we have. So let me talk about my thoughts. So I think I would press the button, assuming it really does stop development everywhere and we can still use the models we have. So, like, regarding the board, I think, like, it kind of misses the mainstream point of discussion. So, like, I think my reason is a bit different from, like, what's written here. And I think, like, what I'm talking about is more of, like, a mainstream. So I think this should be more of, like, the main focus of the board. But, like, I'm kind of worried about what happens if we succeed at building AI that is much smarter than us. So, like, would we actually be able to keep control of it? Honestly, I don't know. And I don't think we should either prove that something will go wrong before taking that seriously. So, Blumo, so this is a message to Blumo. I understand wanting better models for something you've wanted to build for years, but how far does that argument take us? There will always be something the next model could make it possible. At what point would you say, okay, we should understand this one before building the next? The argument that makes me hesitant is medical research. So if better AI could help develop treatment for diseases that we cannot cure today, five years could matter enormously. I wouldn't want to dismiss that. And I think that is what Dario Amodei has been saying. But I also do not know how much of that progress needs more capable models and how much we could get by putting the ones we already have to work. I'd want the both to give us better evidence about where we can control more powerful systems. Five years might not be enough. Still, I'd take the time. So for people who wouldn't pause, I'd like to ask: do you think losing control is unlikely, or do you think the benefits are worth taking the risk? Those would be very different reasons to leave the button alone. Rashik

Using an iMac as an external display
 Common questions
 Can a 5K iMac be used as an external monitor?

 Every way to use a 5K iMac as a monitor 
 Is SecondGlow a Target Display Mode alternative?
 Yes. It does the job Target Display Mode did on older iMacs, in software, for the Retina iMacs from 2015 to 2020: the 27-inch 5K and the 21.5-inch 4K. The iMac stays on and runs SecondGlow too, free, and your Mac treats it as an external display.

 SecondGlow vs RetinaRelay 
 Should I buy a new 5K display instead?
 If you want a camera and microphones, or one cable that also charges your laptop, a new display like Apple’s Studio Display is better, from $1,599. If you already have a 5K iMac and mostly want its screen, SecondGlow gives you that for $39. Try it free for 7 days before you decide.
 SecondGlow vs a new Studio Display

SecondGlow sends a sharp picture with adaptive quality over a USB 3 cable instead, and I measure about 50 to 60 fps on full-screen 5K video.

 How is it different from AirPlay?
 AirPlay to Mac is free and built into macOS, but works over Wi-Fi, and Apple only lists Macs from 2018 or later as receivers, so of the Retina iMacs only the 2019 and 2020 models and the iMac Pro can use it.  Yes, on macOS Sonoma 14.2 or later. Turn on Sound on the iMac in SecondGlow on your Mac: your Mac’s sound plays through the iMac’s speakers in step with the picture, and your Mac’s volume and mute keys control it. Headphones and AirPods on your Mac still work as usual.
 Can I use the iMac’s keyboard or mouse?
 No. Like any display, the iMac shows your Mac’s screen, and keyboard and mouse stay with your Mac.
 Is the picture lossless?
 When the screen is still, yes: every pixel arrives exactly as your Mac drew it. When things move, adaptive quality compresses on the GPU to keep motion smooth, and goes back to lossless a couple of seconds after the screen settles.
 Does the iMac need to be on?
 Yes, with SecondGlow open on it. Turn on automatic login, and the iMac is ready as a display after every restart.
 Is it private?
 Yes. The picture travels only over the cable, encrypted, and never leaves your two Macs. No account. The apps send only a few anonymous setup counts, explained on the privacy page. Questions come straight to me at support@secondglow.app.
 Privacy 
 My Mac says “Unlock to use accessories”. What do I do?
 That’s macOS checking a new USB connection, before SecondGlow is involved. Unlock your Mac, and click Allow if it asks. To plug in while your Mac is locked, open System Settings → Privacy & Security and set Allow accessories to connect to Always.

 English · 简体中文

---

## Philosophy

1. **Kanban organizes human context** — specs, `#Card` references, screenshots, `@Agent` discussions, structured reports, and review gates stay together on each Card.
2. **Herdr drives native Agent CLIs with minimal interference** — run Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity (`agy`), Cursor CLI, or custom CLIs directly inside persistent PTYs with native TUIs, permissions, MCPs, skills, and session resume intact.
3. **Most work stays on Kanban and dispatches via workflows** — shape scope and review diffs on the Board while workflows isolate Git worktrees, dispatch agents, and queue merges automatically.

---

## Highlights

### Kanban for Human

Move Cards across customizable stages (`Backlog → Develop → Review`) with live `@developer`, `@reviewer`, and `@merger` status capsules right on the Board. Each Card combines Markdown specs, pasted screenshots, `#Card` / `#tag` links, `Cmd+O` Quick Open, and GitHub Issue/PR sync with approval gates for external PRs.

### GitHub Actions Style Workflows

Automate column transitions, `@agent` runs, custom scripts, conditions, human approvals, and serialized FIFO **Queue Merge** (`deliver` with automatic `@merger` conflict resolution) inside isolated per-Card Git worktrees — authored visually in Workflow Studio, in YAML, or via **Edit with agent**.

 
 
 

### Herdr Terminal

Press `Cmd+J` on any Card for a side-by-side terminal split or open the dedicated **Terminals** workspace. Built in Rust with `longbridge/nsh` (AppKit/Metal) and `libghostty-vt` over local or remote SSH `herdr-core`, running agent PTYs survive app restarts and upgrades across 17 built-in dark themes.

 
 
 

---

## Installation

**Prerequisites**: macOS 13.0+ (Apple Silicon), `git`, at least one native Agent CLI (`claude`, `codex`, `agy`, `cursor-agent`, etc.), and **Herdr Core (`hc`)** (Canban guides one-click `hc` setup on first launch if missing).

```bash
curl -fsSL https://canban.dev/install.sh | bash
```

Installs or live-upgrades `/Applications/Canban.app` without interrupting active `herdr-core` sessions, and automatically handles macOS Gatekeeper quarantine removal and local ad-hoc code signing.

---

## Related Software and Acknowledgements

Canban builds directly on these open-source projects and assets (full attributions and licenses are preserved in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md):

- **Herdr (`herdr-core`)** — Persistent PTY session supervisor and JSON-RPC runtime powering native Agent CLIs and interactive terminals (Apache-2.0)
- **Sheprd** — Terminal VT/frame/input and subscription utility patterns referenced during integration (Apache-2.0)
- **NSH (`longbridge/nsh`)** — Native macOS AppKit/Metal Rust UI framework (Apache-2.0)
- **Ghostty (`libghostty-vt`)** — Commit-pinned VT parser and terminal emulation engine (MIT)
- **iTerm2-Color-Schemes** (MIT) — 16 classic terminal color palettes including Monokai, Dracula, Nord, Tokyo Night, and Catppuccin Mocha
- **Lucide** (ISC), **Lobe Icons** (MIT), and **Primer Octicons** (MIT) — UI and provider icons

title: Show HN: Skillroll – pure Markdown evals for any skill using a Dungeon Master
author: vafels
body:
Maintaining agentic skills alway felt like a chore due to how hard it was to test them.Writing evals is just too complex to do for every small skill,
So I wrote Skillroll - an eval framework that can test any skill using only an eval.mdHow? instead of setting up an intricate eval environment, you write a short world description, run a Dungeon Master agent that simulates that world, and route all tool calls to that agent.each eval.md is a test case with a "world description", "agent prompt and "judgement criteria" for an llm judge to consider when rating pass/fail.I think Skillroll is especially useful for things like fixing skills by writing a failing eval and iterating on the skill until it passes, 
you can then keep the eval to guard against future regressions and automatically run it in ci.
You can also use it to write new evals using TDD-like approach.I found openai's Luna to be a very nice value-for-money option for running the dungeon master, with cost per eval of around $0.003, and support for pretty complex world scenarios.I hope it might help you reduce the friction in writing evals for your own skills

# raed667/claudette

Claude Code + Mistral = 🧡

- Stars: 1

## Top Contributors

---

## README

# claudette

Run Claude Code with Mistral models.

`claudette` is a drop-in wrapper around `claude`. It starts a small local proxy
that translates Claude Code's requests for Mistral's API, then runs `claude`
against it. It keeps its own config directory, so your regular Claude Code
setup, login and history are left alone.

Anthropic doesn't support running Claude Code on non-Claude models, so treat
this as best-effort. The limitations are listed below.

## Requirements

- Claude Code
- uv
- A Mistral API key from console.mistral.ai

Tested on macOS. Linux should work but hasn't been tested, and Windows isn't
supported.

## Install

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raed667/claudette/main/install.sh | bash
```

The installer asks for your Mistral API key and stores it in
`~/.config/claudette/mistral_api_key`. If you skip the prompt, run the command
again later or export `MISTRAL_API_KEY` instead.

To update, run `claudette update` or the same install command.

## Usage

`claudette` takes the same flags and subcommands as `claude`:

```sh
claudette
claudette -p "explain this repo"
claudette --continue
```

The proxy starts on first use and keeps running in the background. Use
`claudette proxy stop` to shut it down, or `claudette proxy logs` when
requests fail.

The status line shows the model, how much of the context is used before
Claude Code compacts, an estimated cost at Mistral's prices, and the current
folder and branch:

```
mistral-large | ctx 42k/256k 16% | ~$0.96 | claudette (main)
```

The cost is the session's spend so far at Mistral's list prices, cached input
included. It doesn't count web searches or the extra requests auto mode makes
to check tool calls. A trailing `+` means part of the
session used a model without a known price. Mistral doesn't publish one for
Medium, so a Medium-only session shows no cost.

If you've set your own `statusLine` in `~/.claudette/settings.json`, yours is
used instead.

## Models

The main model is `mistral-large-latest`, and background tasks use
`mistral-small-latest`. Any chat model your key can use works.
`claudette models` lists them with their context sizes:

```sh
claudette models
CLAUDETTE_MODEL=ministral-14b-latest claudette
```

The list is cached for a day; `claudette models --refresh` fetches it again.

Large, Medium and Small are the ones that have been tested. Codestral and
`mistral-code-latest` are listed but don't call tools, which Claude Code
depends on.

Inside a session, `/model` lists Large, Medium and Small, plus your
`CLAUDETTE_MODEL` if it's something else, and `/model ` takes any other
model. Compaction is tuned to the model you start with, so prefer
`CLAUDETTE_MODEL` when switching to a model with a smaller context window. If
you've set your own `modelPicker` in `~/.claudette/settings.json`, yours is
used instead.

## Configuration

| Variable | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `MISTRAL_API_KEY` | | Overrides the key file |
| `CLAUDETTE_MODEL` | `mistral-large-latest` | Main model |
| `CLAUDETTE_FAST_MODEL` | `mistral-small-latest` | Background tasks |
| `CLAUDETTE_COMPACT_WINDOW` | model's context, up to `256000` | Tokens before Claude Code compacts the conversation |
| `CLAUDETTE_PORT` | `4791` | Local proxy port |
| `CLAUDETTE_STATUSLINE` | `1` | Set to `0` to turn off the default status line |

## Limitations

- Web search goes through Mistral's own search instead of Anthropic's. You get
 a summarised answer with source links rather than raw results, and searches
 are billed by Mistral.
- Extended thinking, prompt caching, Remote Control, voice mode and fast mode
 aren't available.
- Your global `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is still loaded, which means its contents
 are sent to Mistral.

## Contributing

How it works, testing and known quirks are in CONTRIBUTING.md.

## Disclaimer

claudette is a hobby project. I wanted Claude Code's workflow with Mistral's
models, so I built it for myself and published it in case someone else wants
the same thing. I'm not affiliated with Anthropic or Mistral AI, and neither
company endorses or supports it.

Claude, Claude Code and Mistral are trademarks of their owners. claudette
doesn't include or modify Claude Code; it launches your own install against
Mistral's public API with your own key, so both companies' terms still apply
to how you use them.

# Steamworks.js

A modern implementation of the Steamworks SDK for HTML/JS and NodeJS based applications.

## Why

I used greenworks for a long time and it's great, but I gave up for the following reasons.

- I hate C++.
- The API implement callbacks instead of return flags or promises.
- The API it's not trustful.
- Don't have typescript definitions.
- You have to build the binaries by yourself.
- It's not context-aware.
- It's not up to date.
- It's not being maintained anymore.

## API

```
const steamworks = require('steamworks.js')

// You can pass an appId, or don't pass anything and use a steam_appid.txt file
const client = steamworks.init(480)

// Print Steam username
console.log(client.localplayer.getName())

// Tries to activate an achievement
if (client.achievement.activate('ACHIEVEMENT')) {
    // ...
}
```

You can refer to the declarations file to check the API support and get more detailed documentation of each function.

## Installation

To use steamworks.js you don't have to build anything, just install it from npm:

```
$: npm i steamworks.js
```

### Electron

Steamworks.js is a native module and cannot be used by default in the renderer process. To enable the usage of native modules on the renderer process, the following configurations should be made on`main.js`:

```
const mainWindow = new BrowserWindow({
    // ...
    webPreferences: {
        // ...
        contextIsolation: false,
        nodeIntegration: true
    }
})
```

To make the steam overlay working, call the`electronEnableSteamOverlay` on the end of your`main.js` file:

```
require('steamworks.js').electronEnableSteamOverlay()
```

For the production build, copy the relevant distro files from`sdk/redistributable_bin/{YOUR_DISTRO}` into the root of your build. If you are using electron-forge, look for#75.

## How to build

You only need to build if you are going to change something on steamworks.js code, if you are looking to just consume the library or use it in your game, refer to the installation section.

Make sure you have the latest node.js, Rust and Clang. We also need Steam installed and running.

Install dependencies with`npm install` and then run`npm run build:debug` to build the library.

There is no way to build for all targets easily. The good news is that you don't need to. You can develop and test on your current target, and open a PR. When the code is merged to main, a github action will build for all targets and publish a new version.

### Testing Electron

Go to the test/electron directory. There, you can run`npm install` and then`npm start` to run the Electron app.

Click "activate overlay" to test the overlay.
