title: Show HN: profiler-md converts performance profiles to Markdown
author: tomeraberbach
body: Hi HN!profiler-md is a CLI and JS library that converts performance profiles to Markdown across 17 formats (e.g. pprof), 29 profilers (e.g. py-spy), 22 languages (e.g. Rust), and 4 profile types (call stack profiles, call graphs, heap snapshots, and traces).Earlier this year I tried using AI agents for performance optimization. They weren't very effective because they frequently:- Speculated about why something was slow from just reading the code- Made changes, measured the wall time before vs after, and struggled to distinguish real improvements from noise- Analyzed raw profiles using one-off scripts, which were often subtly incorrectThe issue was that the agents couldn't read a flamegraph like I could. In a flamegraph, I could see what was slow, and when I made changes, I could see whether the targeted work was eliminated. The agents needed a feedback loop like that.So I wrote a small converter from Node CPU profiles to Markdown. The agents were much more effective when using it, and I realized I also liked reading the Markdown myself!I felt this had potential, and I use many different programming languages at work, so I decided to build profiler-md. I also wrote an agent skill [1], which I've successfully used to optimize profiler-md itself and its pprof-format dependency (a 78x speedup on a large pprof file [2] and a 3.3x speedup more broadly [3]).I got to solve some fun problems for this project:- Making it so that adding a new format, profiler, or profile type is as simple as implementing an interface and adding to a registry. body: Hi HN, I made Pizza, an open-source, event-driven AI agent. No `while true`.Each turn is a state machine. Conversations and tool calls go into an immutable SQLite log. The UI, model context, and session tree are built from that log.The model gets one tool: a CLI. Reading files, editing code, and running commands all go through it.You can keep a conversation going without manually starting new sessions. Pizza compacts context as needed, and you can branch from any earlier message.Agents in separate workspaces talk through `tell`, each doing the work in its own project. An SSH host can be a workspace too: Pizza deploys itself there and runs remotely.Desktop and terminal interfaces are included. Bring your own model.https://github.com/pizza-agent/pizza

title: Show HN: Simple tool for FDEs to avoid missing HITL steps in claude code
author: rdelgadoferr
body:
# robertodf99/hook-me-up

Answer Claude Code from native macOS notifications: approve permissions, answer questions and plans, and know when a session finishes. One-line install.

- Stars: 0
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 0
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-11-14T16:43:02Z

## Languages

- JavaScript
- Makefile
- Shell
- Swift

## Topics

- claude-code
- claude-code-hooks
- claude-code-plugin
- developer-tools
- hooks
- macos
- macos-app
- notifications
- swift

## Top Contributors

- robertodf99 (38 contributions)

---

## README

# Hook Me Up

 

Answer Claude Code from native macOS notifications. When Claude Code needs permission
for a tool, asks you a question, wants a plan approved or finishes a turn, Hook Me Up
shows a notification you can act on right there: approve or deny, pick an answer,
approve the plan or ask for changes. Click the notification to jump to the session.
It is built on Claude Code's hooks and fails open: if anything is off, Claude Code
simply shows its usual terminal dialog.

Claude Code asks for permission and you approve or deny it from a macOS notification, pick an answer to its question or open Reply… for every option plus a box for your own, then click a notification to jump to its session

## Install

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robertodf99/hook-me-up/main/install.sh | bash
```

The installer downloads the latest release (and checks its SHA-256), installs
`~/Applications/Hook Me Up.app`, shows the changes it would make to
`~/.claude/settings.json` and **asks before writing them** (with a timestamped
backup), adds the editor extension to VS Code, VS Code Insiders,
Cursor and Windsurf when it finds their command-line tool, and starts the menu-bar agent
at login. Run it again to upgrade.

Uninstall:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robertodf99/hook-me-up/main/uninstall.sh | bash
```

It stops the agent, removes Hook Me Up's hooks from your settings (again after showing
the diff and asking), and removes the app, its support folder and the editor extension
(with each editor's command-line tool it finds). Your settings backups stay where they
are.

Requirements: macOS 14 or later, and Claude Code.

### Install from Claude Code

Hook Me Up is also a Claude Code plugin with three commands that run the same installer
and ask for your confirmation in the chat:

```text
/plugin marketplace add robertodf99/hook-me-up
/plugin install hook-me-up@hook-me-up
```

(On Claude Code 2.1.275 or later, `/plugin install hook-me-up --marketplace robertodf99/hook-me-up`
does both in one step.) Then:

- `/hook-me-up:install` installs or upgrades Hook Me Up: it shows the changes to
 `~/.claude/settings.json` and adds the hooks only after you say yes.
- `/hook-me-up:doctor` checks the installation and explains how to fix what is off.
- `/hook-me-up:uninstall` shows what would be removed and removes it after you say yes.

The plugin has commands only, no hooks: the hooks live in `~/.claude/settings.json` as
with the installer. Hooks inside the plugin would run in addition to those, and every
request would be notified twice.

### First run

Once the agent runs, the installer waits (up to a minute in a terminal, 10 seconds
without one) for you to answer macOS's question about notifications, shows a test
notification, and tells you what is left to do:

1. Allow notifications for **Hook Me Up** when macOS asks (or in System Settings →
 Notifications → Hook Me Up).
2. In the same place, set the style to **Alerts**, so requests stay on screen until
 you answer them. On a first install, the installer opens System Settings at
 Notifications when the style isn't Alerts yet; on an upgrade, only when
 notifications are off.
3. Restart Claude Code sessions that were already running, so they load the hooks.

## What you'll see

| When Claude Code… | Notification | Actions, in order |
|---|---|---|
| needs permission for a tool | `project · Needs permission`, with a plain-language summary and warnings such as "⚠︎ Leaves your machine" | Approve, Deny, Approve for session (when Claude Code suggests a session rule) |
| asks a question with up to four options | `project · Question` | One action per option, then Reply… for your own answer |
| asks a question with more options, or a multi-select one | `project · Question`, the options numbered in the body | Reply…: type `2`, `1, 3`, or an option's label |
| wants a plan approved | `project · Plan to approve`, with the first lines of the plan | Approve plan, Request changes… (your text goes back to Claude) |
| finishes a turn, or waits for a reply | `project · Finished` / `Waiting for your reply` | none |

- **Clicking a notification opens its session**: Terminal and iTerm2 select the exact
 tab. Ghostty (1.3 or later) focuses the terminal whose working directory is the folder
 Claude Code was started in. When several terminals are there (splits or tabs in the
 same folder), Hook Me Up briefly sets the title of the session's own terminal to a
 random marker, asks Ghostty which terminal shows it, puts the old title back and
 focuses that terminal; the title is back within about a second. When Ghostty doesn't
 show the marker in time (a fixed `title = …` in its config, or the session changed its
 title first), the title is cleared instead, so no marker is left behind (a title the
 session set meanwhile shows again when it next sets one), and Ghostty just comes to
 the front, as it does when the session has ended, when no terminal is in the folder, or
 when Ghostty's AppleScript is off (`macos-applescript = false`).
 VS Code and Cursor (and VS Code Insiders and Windsurf) focus the open window that
 contains the folder Claude Code was started in: that folder's window, the window of
 the repository a worktree or subfolder belongs to, or a saved `.code-workspace` that
 includes it; with the editor extension, the session's integrated
 terminal is shown too, even when the window has several. While the session's window is
 open, a click opens no new window; when no open window contains the folder, the editor
 just comes to the front (and, with the extension, the front window shows the session's
 terminal if it has it). The editor keeps its list of windows up to date with a delay,
 so right after you close windows a click may just bring the editor to the front. Zed and
 other apps come to the front.
 The click hands the request to Claude Code's terminal dialog: nothing is
 approved or answered from it. In a multi-question flow, the answers given so far are
 dropped and the terminal asks all the questions again.
- macOS shows the **first action as a button** and the others under **Options** when
 you hover the notification, so the most likely answer comes first.
- Several questions arrive one at a time; Claude gets all the answers after the last.
 A reply that can't be understood brings the question back with a hint.
- Answering needs an unlocked Mac, so nothing can be approved from the lock screen.
- Notifications are grouped per repository, play the default sound once, and
 disappear when the request is answered (here or in the terminal), cancelled, or the
 session moves on.

The ✻ menu-bar item shows how many requests are waiting and offers **Pause for 30
minutes**, **Resume** and **Quit**.

### Editor extension

VS Code can't be asked from outside which integrated terminal runs a session, so Hook Me
Up comes with a small extension for VS Code, VS Code Insiders, Cursor and Windsurf (plain
JavaScript, no dependencies; source in editor-extension/). On a
click, the agent writes a request to
`~/Library/Application Support/hook-me-up/editor-focus-request.json`: a random id, the
time and the session's process ids, nothing else (no paths, titles or commands). Every
editor window watches that file; the window with a terminal whose process is one of those
ids shows it, and the others do nothing. Without the extension (or with it disabled), a
click works exactly as before: it focuses the window.

- The installer adds it with each editor's command-line tool (`code`, `code-insiders`,
 `cursor`, `windsurf`, on your `PATH` or inside the app in `/Applications` or
 `~/Applications`) and says so; if adding it fails, the install goes on. Set
 `HOOK_ME_UP_NO_EDITOR_EXTENSION=1` to skip it.
- Windows that were already open may need a reload (**Developer: Reload Window**) before
 the extension runs in them.
- The uninstaller removes it. You can also remove it from the editor's Extensions view
 (it is "Hook Me Up", id `hook-me-up.hook-me-up`).
- `hook-me-up-setup doctor` shows which editors have it (an INFO line; it never fails).
- Profiles: Hook Me Up checks the extension in the default profile's list (where the
 installer adds it). A window that uses another profile runs it only if that profile has
 it too; otherwise the click focuses that window as before.

## How it works

```
Claude Code ──hook──▶ hook-me-up ──Unix socket──▶ Hook Me Up (menu-bar agent)
     ▲                    │                              │
     └──── decision ◀─────┘ ◀──────── your answer ◀──── native notification
```

Claude Code runs the `hook-me-up` command for `PermissionRequest`, `Notification`,
`Stop`, `UserPromptSubmit` and `SessionEnd`. For a permission request, the hook asks
the agent over a local socket and waits; the agent shows a notification and sends back
your decision, and the hook prints it for Claude Code. If there is no decision (the
agent isn't running, notifications are off, the agent is paused, something fails, or
the request times out), the hook prints nothing and Claude Code shows its own terminal
dialog. You can always answer in the terminal instead; the notification then goes
away. See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md for the details.

## Security model

- **Fail-open.** The hook outputs a decision only when you made one. Errors never turn
 into an approval or a denial.
- **Local, same-user socket.** The socket lives in a private folder (`0700`, socket
 `0600`) and both sides check that the peer runs as the same user (`getpeereid`).
- **One answer per request.** Every request has its own id; the agent answers only on
 that request's connection, at most once, and the hook ignores any answer for another
 id. An action only counts if it belongs to the notification currently shown.
- **The hook builds the output.** Answers never carry tool input from the agent: the
 hook builds `updatedInput` from its own `tool_input`.
- **Session-only rules.** "Approve for session" keeps only rule and directory
 suggestions and always scopes them to the session; it never writes to your settings.
- **Unlocked Mac only** for every answering action.
- **Clicks reach only the session's own terminal.** For Ghostty, the title marker is
 written only to the session's tty, and only while the session runs and that tty is
 still its controlling terminal (a character device of yours with the same device
 number, opened without following links); the marker is random, goes to Ghostty's
 AppleScript as an argument (never as script text), and the title written back has no
 control characters. The editor extension acts only on a request that is exactly what
 the agent writes: a file of yours in your private support folder, not a link, at most
 4 KiB, less than 5 seconds old, each id once, 1 to 16 process ids; it never writes the
 file, logs nothing and sends nothing anywhere.
- **Careful installer.** It verifies the package checksum, shows the settings diff and
 asks first, backs up, writes atomically, and refuses to write if the file changed
 meanwhile.
- **No content in logs.** `~/Library/Logs/hook-me-up.log` and the unified log (subsystem
 `io.github.robertodf99.hook-me-up`) hold event kinds and short ids only.

## Why macOS says "unidentified developer"

Hook Me Up is signed ad-hoc: it has no Apple Developer ID and is not notarized. A
Developer ID is a paid Apple membership, and this project won't buy one. What you see
because of that:

- System Settings → General → Login Items (Login Items & Extensions on newer macOS)
 lists Hook Me Up under **Allow in the Background**, marked as from an unidentified
 developer.
- When the installer starts the agent, macOS may show a notice that Hook Me Up added
 an item that can run in the background. That is the LaunchAgent that starts the
 agent at login.
- `codesign -dv ~/Applications/"Hook Me Up.app"` shows `Signature=adhoc`.

**Why the install isn't blocked.** Gatekeeper checks apps that carry the quarantine
flag (`com.apple.quarantine`), which browsers and other apps add to what they download.
`curl` doesn't add it, so the app the installer unpacks opens normally. The same zip
downloaded with a browser would be quarantined, and Gatekeeper would block the app from
opening.

**What to do.** Keep the Login Items entry enabled: turning it off stops the agent from
starting at login, and requests then go to the terminal dialog. Install with the script
rather than by downloading the zip in a browser. Or build it yourself from this
repository (Building from source).

**How to check what you installed.**

- `codesign --verify --strict --deep ~/Applications/"Hook Me Up.app"` checks that no
 file changed since the package was signed. An ad-hoc signature can't tell you who
 signed it.
- The installer compares the zip with the `.sha256` file published in the same
 release. That catches a corrupted or cut-short download. It doesn't protect against
 a compromised account or release: whoever can replace the zip can replace its
 checksum too.
- Releases from v0.2.0 on carry a GitHub build provenance attestation, which ties the
 zip to the workflow run and the commit that built it:

  ```sh
  gh release download v0.2.0 --repo robertodf99/hook-me-up --pattern '*.zip'
  gh attestation verify hook-me-up-0.2.0-macos.zip --repo robertodf99/hook-me-up \
    --signer-workflow robertodf99/hook-me-up/.github/workflows/release.yml
  # Compare it with the installed app:
  ditto -x -k hook-me-up-0.2.0-macos.zip unpacked
  diff -r unpacked/HookMeUp.app ~/Applications/"Hook Me Up.app"
  ```

 This shows the zip was built by this repository's release workflow from that
 commit. It says nothing about what the code at that commit does: reading the source,
 or building it yourself, is still the strongest check.

## Configuration

The installer and uninstaller read these environment variables:

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `HOOK_ME_UP_VERSION=v1.2.3` | Install that release instead of the latest |
| `HOOK_ME_UP_YES=1` | Change `~/.claude/settings.json` without asking (non-interactive installs) |
| `HOOK_ME_UP_ZIP= ` | Install a local package (its `.sha256` must sit next to it) |
| `HOOK_ME_UP_NO_ONBOARDING=1` | Skip the notification check after starting the agent (no waiting, no test notification, System Settings stays closed) |
| `HOOK_ME_UP_NO_EDITOR_EXTENSION=1` | Don't add the editor extension to VS Code, VS Code Insiders, Cursor or Windsurf |

Example: `curl -fsSL …/install.sh | HOOK_ME_UP_YES=1 bash`. Without a terminal and
without `HOOK_ME_UP_YES=1`, the installer changes nothing in your settings and prints
the command to run.

To take a break, use **Pause for 30 minutes** in the menu bar: requests go to the
terminal until it ends or you choose **Resume**.

## Building from source

Requires Xcode 16 or later (Swift 6).

```sh
make            # build the hook, the installer CLI and the agent
make test       # unit tests
make lint       # swift format lint (make format to apply)
make app        # .build/HookMeUp.app (with the editor extension in Contents/Resources)
make vsix       # the editor extension alone: .build/hook-me-up.vsix
make install    # package this checkout and run install.sh with it
make uninstall  # run uninstall.sh
make dist VERSION=1.2.3 UNIVERSAL=1   # .build/dist/hook-me-up-1.2.3-macos.zip and .sha256
```

docs/TESTING.md lists the automated checks and a manual end-to-end
checklist. Pushing a `v*` tag publishes a release with GitHub Actions.

## Troubleshooting

Start with the doctor. It checks the app, the LaunchAgent, the running agent, the hooks in
`~/.claude/settings.json` and the notification settings, and says how to fix each
problem (it changes nothing itself):

```sh
~/Applications/"Hook Me Up.app"/Contents/MacOS/hook-me-up-setup doctor
```

From Claude Code, run `/hook-me-up:doctor`.

The agent writes its log to `~/Library/Logs/hook-me-up.log`.

- **No notifications.** Check System Settings → Notifications → Hook Me Up. While
 notifications are off, every request goes to the terminal and the log says how to
 turn them on.
- **Nothing happens at all.** Make sure the agent runs (✻ in the menu bar; else run the
 installer again) and restart your Claude Code sessions so they load the hooks.
- **The agent's folder was deleted** (`~/Library/Application Support/hook-me-up`, say by
 a cleanup tool): the agent notices within about 5 seconds, creates it again and keeps
 listening (the log says `socket was removed or replaced; listening again`). Requests in
 between go to the terminal.
- **The icon is out of date** after an upgrade. macOS caches it:

  ```sh
  /System/Library/Frameworks/CoreServices.framework/Frameworks/LaunchServices.framework/Support/lsregister -f ~/Applications/"Hook Me Up.app"
  killall NotificationCenter usernoted
  ```

 If it is still stale, log out and back in.
- **Login Items shows "unidentified developer".** Releases are signed ad-hoc; keep the
 item enabled. See Why macOS says "unidentified developer"
 for what that means and how to check what you installed.
- **Clicking a notification doesn't select the tab.** The first time, macOS asks to let
 Hook Me Up control Terminal, iTerm2 or Ghostty; allow it in System Settings → Privacy &
 Security → Automation. With several Ghostty terminals in the session's folder, the log
 says why one wasn't picked (`ghostty: title marker not seen`, for instance when
 Ghostty's config sets `title`). In VS Code and the editors built on it, the terminal is
 shown only with the editor extension: check it with the doctor, and
 reload windows opened before it was installed.

## Feedback

Tried it? Tell me what worked and what broke in
Feedback & ideas; questions go to
Q&A. For a bug,
open an issue with the output
of `hook-me-up-setup doctor`.

The app icon is drawn from the Claude symbol on Wikimedia Commons (CC0 1.0); see
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.

title: Show HN: Nostalgia Rider
author: qvq
body:
Nostalgia-Rider is a browser toy that mashes up Line Rider [1] and Ski Stunt Simulator [2]. I loved to play both back when they were popular and thought it would be fun to create this.No accounts or ads. It's a pure static site.[1] https://www.linerider.com
[2] https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~van/sssjava/javademo.html

comments.author: qvq
comments.text: Technical details:I did pay attention to performance, even if it's overkill. Uses Zig compiled to WASM for the game state. Rendering is done in JS and WebGL reading from SharedArrayBuffer. I didn't think a single language was worth the boundary trampolining and extra tooling.I tried to get muti-threading to work but that seems to require multiple web workers running instances of the WASM binary. It started to make other things more complicated (probably because I couldn't find the right level of abstraction) so I gave up. Running WASM in a single worker, off the main thread, is good enough for now.

title: Show HN: Folate – Local DOM selector model that beats 7B VLMs at 1/60th the size
author: asernasr
body:
# figranium/folate

A lightweight, CPU-efficient neural DOM element ranker built for browser automation

- Stars: 1
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 1
- Open issues: 1
- License: Apache License 2.0
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-11-14T12:25:04Z

## Languages

- Python

## Top Contributors

- asernasr (32 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 PyPI •
 Hugging Face •
 Demo •
 Apache 2.0 
 

 
 A lightweight, CPU-efficient neural DOM element ranker built for browser automation within tight memory constraints (<2 GB total footprint alongside a headless browser).
 

Fine-tuned from `google/electra-base-discriminator` on `osunlp/Mind2Web` and dynamically quantized to **INT8 ONNX (~107 MB)**, Folate runs purely via `onnxruntime` and `tokenizers`—requiring no PyTorch or `transformers` at inference time.

---

## Model Overview

Folate operates as a discriminative cross-encoder that scores `(natural_language_query, serialized_dom_element)` pairs in a single batched forward pass on CPU.

| Variant / Artifact | Backbone | Precision / Format | Disk Size | Runtime RAM |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`folate-int8` (Default)** | `google/electra-base-discriminator` | Dynamic `QUInt8` ONNX | ~107 MB | ~180–250 MB |
| **`folate-base`** | `google/electra-base-discriminator` | `float32` Safetensors | ~418 MB | ~1.4+ GB (PyTorch) |

### Key Capabilities

* **Zero-Hallucination Selector Grounding** — Ranks real interactive DOM nodes extracted via `lxml` XPath (` `, ` `, ` `, ` `, ` `, ARIA interactive roles, and `onclick`/`tabindex` elements), guaranteeing every returned CSS/XPath selector exists on the live page.
* **Compact Structured Serialization** — Serializes each element into a concise `96`-token representation:
 `[TAG] ... [ID/NAME/TYPE/ROLE/ARIA-LABEL/PLACEHOLDER/TITLE/ALT/HREF/DATA-TESTID] ... [TEXT] ... [PARENT] ...`
* **Edge & Low-Memory Deployment** — Designed to run alongside Chromium on resource-constrained laptops and containers without GPU acceleration.

---

## Quickstart

### Installation

```bash
pip install folate
```

Or install from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/figranium/folate
cd folate
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

To run the live browser examples with Playwright:

```bash
python -m pip install -r examples/requirements.txt
python -m playwright install chromium
```

### Usage

`FolateSelectorFinder` automatically downloads and caches `figranium/folate` on first run (or loads `./folate-int8` if present locally):

```python
from folate import FolateSelectorFinder

finder = FolateSelectorFinder()
matches = finder.rank("click Search Flights button", html_source, top_k=3)

for match in matches:
    print(f"{match['score']:.4f} | {match['selector']} | {match['element']}")
```

To load weights from a custom local directory:

```python
finder = FolateSelectorFinder(model_dir="./folate-int8")
```

### Programmatic Model Download

If you want to pre-fetch the quantized model weights via `huggingface_hub`:

```bash
hf download figranium/folate --local-dir ./folate-int8
```

---

## Repository Structure

```text
folate/
├── folate/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── ranker.py                  # Lightweight CPU inference engine & DOM serializer
├── scripts/
│   ├── prepare_data.py            # Streaming Mind2Web serializer (lxml)
│   ├── train.py                   # Fine-tuning script (bf16/fp16/CPU)
│   ├── export_onnx.py             # FP32 ONNX export + INT8 dynamic quantization
│   ├── eval_mind2web.py           # Official Mind2Web evaluator (Precision/Recall/F1, Top-1/3/5 & MRR)
│   └── eval_precision.py          # Playwright DOM-resolved selector Precision & Recall benchmark
├── examples/
│   ├── test_google.py             # Live Playwright search box grounding on google.com
│   ├── test_amazon.py             # E-commerce element ranking on amazon.com (+ offline snapshot)
│   ├── test_github.py             # Repository navigation grounding on github.com
│   └── requirements.txt           # Optional Playwright dependency for live browser tests
├── requirements.txt               # Lightweight CPU runtime dependencies
├── requirements-train.txt         # Training & ONNX export dependencies
└── LICENSE
```

---

## Evaluation & Benchmarks

Folate is evaluated on the three standard generalization splits of **Mind2Web** (`test_task`, `test_website`, and `test_domain`) across **6,037 action steps** on real-world webpages.

### Mind2Web Results (INT8 ONNX · CPU)

| Split | Description | Steps | Avg Candidates | Top-1 | Top-3 | Top-5 | MRR | Avg Latency (2 vCPU) |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **`test_task`** | Unseen tasks on seen websites | 1,256 | 50.0 | **93.31%** | 97.61% | 98.33% | 0.9566 | 2,309.9 ms/step |
| **`test_website`** | Completely unseen websites | 955 | 50.0 | **88.90%** | 95.92% | 96.65% | 0.9274 | 4,328.2 ms/step |
| **`test_domain`** | Unseen domains & verticals | 3,826 | 49.8 | **92.08%** | 97.28% | 98.61% | 0.9491 | 2,431.0 ms/step |

### Methodology & Setup

* **Task Formulation:** At each step, the model receives the natural-language task instruction, action history context, and up to **50 candidate DOM elements** (`Avg Candidates ≈ 50.0`) extracted from the page snapshot, and outputs a relevance logit per candidate.
* **Metrics:**
 * **Top-1 / Top-3 / Top-5:** Percentage of steps where a ground-truth target node (`pos_candidates`) appears within the top *k* ranked elements.
 * **Precision / Recall / F1:** Selective Top-1 precision (`TP / (TP + FP)`) and recall (`TP / Total`) across confidence probability thresholds (`--confidence-threshold`, `--thresholds`), plus candidate-level binary precision/recall.
 * **MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank):** Average reciprocal rank for the highest-ranked ground-truth element across all evaluated steps.
* **Hardware & Runtime:** Latency is measured end-to-end per step on **2 vCPUs** with **no GPU acceleration**, using the exported INT8 quantized ONNX artifact (`onnxruntime`). Variance between `test_website` (`4,328.2 ms/step`) and `test_domain` (`2,431.0 ms/step`) reflects longer tokenized DOM attribute sequences on unseen site templates rather than candidate count.

### Comparison with GPT-6 Luna

For context against a fast, cost-efficient frontier LLM, **GPT-6 Luna** (via OpenAI's Decisions API) scores **81.8%** on **Mind2Web Multimodal** (Google Gemini Decision 1 evaluation, Nov 2026) and **81.2%** on **Mind2Web** in the Decision Index Vision suite (Nace.AI, Nov 2026), with ~326 ms median cloud API latency and ~$0.10 per 1,000 decisions (or $0.10 / $0.50 per 1M input/output tokens in standard API usage).

| Model | Type | Mind2Web Accuracy | Deployment & Runtime | Cost |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **Folate (`folate-int8`)** | Specialized DOM Cross-Encoder (~107 MB) | **88.90% – 93.31%** Top-1 (91.83% overall across 6,037 steps) | 100% local CPU (`onnxruntime`, 180–250 MB RAM) | **$0** (self-hosted) |
| **GPT-6 Luna** | Frontier LLM (Decisions API) | 81.2% – 81.8% (Mind2Web Multimodal / Vision) | Cloud API (~326 ms median latency) | ~$0.10 / 1k decisions |

> **Note:** Folate is evaluated on text-based Mind2Web DOM candidates (50 candidates/step), whereas GPT-6 Luna's 81.2%–81.8% scores are on multimodal/screenshot-based Mind2Web action selection. While GPT-6 Luna is a general-purpose frontier model capable of broad reasoning and multi-step planning, Folate's task-specific ELECTRA cross-encoder achieves higher single-step DOM element grounding accuracy locally on CPU with zero API cost, zero network dependency, and zero selector hallucination.

---

## Examples

Run any of the included live browser examples from the repository root:

```bash
python examples/test_google.py
python examples/test_amazon.py --offline
python examples/test_github.py
```

---

## Training & Quantization Pipeline

To reproduce data preparation, fine-tuning, INT8 ONNX export, and evaluation from scratch on `osunlp/Mind2Web`:

```bash
python -m pip install -r requirements-train.txt

# 1. Stream and serialize Mind2Web pairs
python scripts/prepare_data.py --output-dir ./data

# 2. Fine-tune ELECTRA cross-encoder
python scripts/train.py --data-dir ./data --save-dir ./folate-base

# 3. Export to FP32 ONNX and quantize to INT8 (~107 MB)
python scripts/export_onnx.py --model-dir ./folate-base --output-dir ./folate-int8

# 4. Evaluate Mind2Web test splits (Precision, Recall, F1, Top-1/3/5 & MRR)
python scripts/eval_mind2web.py --confidence-threshold 0.5 --json-out mind2web_results.json

# 5. Run Playwright DOM-resolved selector Precision & Recall benchmark
python scripts/eval_precision.py --confidence-threshold 0.5 --json-out precision_results.json
```

---

## Intended Use & Limitations

* **Intended Use:** Single-step natural-language UI element grounding (`click`, `type`, `select`, `hover`) in local browser automation pipelines where RAM and CPU budgets are constrained.
* **Limitations:**
 * **No Multi-Step Planning:** Folate ranks candidate elements for a single action query; it does not plan multi-step workflows or parse unstructured page content.
 * **Local DOM Context Only:** Elements are serialized using their own attributes, inner text, and immediate `[PARENT]` tag—identical sibling elements without distinguishing attributes or text cannot be disambiguated visually.

---

# ArchLog — Engineering Institutional Memory

title: Show HN: ArchLog – a memory for your team's engineering decisions
author: ArchLog
body:
ArchLog — Engineering Institutional Memory

# Explore the context behind an engineering decision.

Engineering systems accumulate decisions, compromises, migrations, incidents and discussions. ArchLog connects that history across code, documentation and team conversations into a searchable engineering memory - so the reasoning survives longer than the people who made it.

Free to connect · Read-only by default · Nothing pushed without your approval

Decision Ledger entry

decision Decision

What was actually decided, stated in one line.

reason Reason

Why it made sense at the time - the part version control never keeps.

impact Impact

What changed as a result, in code and in operational behaviour.

risk · confidence Risk & confidence

How risky the change was, and how strongly the evidence supports the reading.

commits · pull requests Provenance

The commits, pull requests, authors and files the entry was derived from.

## Watch ArchLog turn a workspace’s history into a decision record.

Press play on a simulated workspace: GitHub, Slack and Linear connect, the history of one change—an incident, a Slack thread, commits and a reviewed pull request—streams in, and ArchLog links it into one Decision Ledger entry. Then it answers a question about that entry eight months later, citing every source.

1. 01 Connect
2. 02 Stream
3. 03 Analyze
4. 04 Ledger
5. 05 Ask

No sign-up required · Illustrative data · Pause, skip or ask your own questions

## Your code survives. Your reasoning doesn’t.

What gets lost isn’t the decision. It’s why the decision made sense. Version control preserves what changed; it rarely preserves why. When an engineer leaves, a system grows complex, or an incident forces a rewrite, the reasoning behind the original decision is usually the first thing lost - and the hardest thing to reconstruct.

- Why was this architecture chosen?
- What alternatives were considered, and why were they rejected?
- Why did we migrate authentication?
- What evidence supported the decision at the time?
- What changed after the incident?
- Who needs this context now that the author has left?

These are answerable questions. The evidence already exists - scattered across commits, pull requests, documents and threads nobody has time to read.

## Ask why. Follow the reasoning back to its source.

ArchLog doesn’t just answer what happened. It shows the decision, the context around it, and where each piece came from.

Simulation Simulated workspace · illustrative data · no real accounts connected

▶ Play Restart

1× 2× 4×

Skip to end

0:00 / 1:40

01 Connect 02 Stream 03 Analyze 04 Ledger 05 Ask

Press Play to watch ArchLog connect a simulated workspace, read its history as it arrives, and turn it into one Decision Ledger entry - then answer a question about it eight months later. About 100 seconds at 1×.

### Sources · Acme Payments (simulated)

- GitHub acme/payments-api Not connected
- Slack#payments-eng Not connected
- Linear Payments team Not connected

### Live feed 0 events

Events appear here once sources connect.

### Decision Ledger entry 

No decision detected yet.

## Four stages, in the order they run.

1. 01

### Connect

Sign in with GitHub and connect the systems that already hold your engineering context - repositories, and optionally Slack, Notion and Linear. ArchLog reads them with your own OAuth tokens.
2. 02

### Capture

Commits, pull requests, discussions and documents are analyzed in one pass. The decisions that actually mattered are extracted into a structured Decision Ledger, linked to the code and conversations behind them.
3. 03

### Search

Ask why something is the way it is. Answers can include supporting decisions, commits, or documents. Check the sources and reasoning; AI answers can be incomplete or wrong.
4. 04

### Preserve

The reasoning stays with the organization, not the individual. When someone leaves, what they decided and why remains searchable by whoever inherits the system.

## A decision is a record, not a message in a thread.

Entries organize extracted reasoning, risk, people and affected code. Review the linked evidence for context the extraction may have missed.

- Risk and milestone flags surface the changes that mattered
- Authors, commits and affected files travel with the decision
- Extraction confidence is shown, never hidden behind a summary

payments-api / Decision Ledger

High risk Milestone Confidence 0.86

### Move settlement writes behind an idempotency key

Context

Retries during a provider outage double-charged 14 settlements.

Decision

Every write carries a caller-supplied key; replays return the original result.

3 commits PR #1284 7 files 2 authors

## A document goes stale. A repository does not.

ArchLog reads the system itself - the commits, the pull requests, the files that changed - so context stays attached to the code rather than to a wiki page nobody updated.

- Indexed directly from the repository, not transcribed by hand
- Re-indexed as the system changes
- Every claim links back to the file or commit it came from

Repository

acme/payments-api Indexed

1,204 files 38 decisions 6 milestones

- `src/settlement/writer.ts` 4 decisions
- `src/settlement/retry.ts` 2 decisions
- `migrations/0142_idempotency.sql` 1 decision

## Read a system's evolution in order.

Decisions are organised chronologically, so the shape of a migration - what was tried, what was reversed, what finally held - is legible instead of scattered across two years of pull requests.

- Chronological ledger per repository
- Milestones separated from routine change
- Reversals stay visible rather than being overwritten

Timeline

1. Mar 2026 Settlement writes made idempotent
2. Jan 2026 Retry backoff moved to the queue
3. Nov 2025 In-process retry loop — reversed
4. Aug 2025 Provider split into its own service

## Ask the codebase why.

Search spans decisions, files and connected sources at once. Results are typed and source-backed, so an answer can be followed to the thing that produced it.

- Decisions, files and sources in one result set
- Every result carries its origin
- Relevance is scored separately from extraction confidence

why do settlements retry?

- Decision Move settlement writes behind an idempotency key payments-api · PR #1284
- File`src/settlement/retry.ts` payments-api · indexed
- Decision Retry backoff moved to the queue payments-api · 3 commits

## Connect the systems that already hold the context

ArchLog reads the engineering systems your team already uses. Sources marked as planned are not available yet.

- GitHub Available Repositories, commits, pull requests
- Slack Available Channel discussions and decisions
- Notion Available Design docs, RFCs and specs
- Linear Available Issues, projects and cycles
- Jira Planned Not available yet
- Google Docs Planned Not available yet
- E Excel Planned Not available yet
- Zoom Meetings Planned Not available yet

## Engineering history is sensitive. It’s treated that way.

Your decisions, source context and team conversations are among the most sensitive data an engineering organization holds. Below is what ArchLog actually implements today - no certifications are claimed.

- ### Your own OAuth tokens

ArchLog reads only what you explicitly connect, using your own OAuth grant - and never pushes to your default branch on its own.
- ### Tokens encrypted at rest

Stored integration credentials use application-level encryption. Credentials must still be available to the service when it contacts providers.
- ### Authenticated, origin-scoped API

Account and workspace routes use session authentication. Session cookies are HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax, and marked Secure in production. Some public and provider-callback routes do not require a session.
- ### Verified OAuth and webhooks

Sign-in callbacks validate OAuth state, and supported webhook handlers check provider signatures. Review the requested provider permissions before connecting.

## Answers to what teams ask first

Does ArchLog store my source code?

ArchLog indexes structural metadata - file paths, imports, symbols, dependency graphs, and analysis results - in its own database. Generated documentation, patches, evidence and connected-source records can contain code or other source content. Relevant content may be sent to the configured AI provider.

What does ArchLog have access to?

Only what your OAuth tokens grant for the sources you explicitly connect. ArchLog never pushes to your default branch - patch suggestions are always proposed as a diff you review and approve, never applied automatically.

How is this different from asking an LLM about my code?

A raw LLM only sees the code you paste in, at that moment. ArchLog first builds a structured record of your engineering history, then uses that record to help explain engineering choices. Its interpretations still need your review.

Which languages does it support?

Structural analysis (imports, symbols, complexity) currently covers JavaScript/TypeScript and Python most deeply; the Decision Ledger, chat, and documentation features work across any language since they're driven by commit/PR history and file structure, not just per-language parsing.

What happens if I disconnect a source?

Disconnecting is not a data-deletion request. Previously stored records may remain; contact us about removing them.

## Keep the reasoning, not just the result.

Connect a repository and see what your own history has been trying to tell you.

Drag a placed piece on the board to move or swap it, or click it (or drag it off the board) to return it to the tray.

title: Show HN: Panel – A research workspace where the agent can build its own panes
author: greentfrapp
body:
# greentfrapp/panel

- Stars: 78
- Forks: 7
- Watchers: 78
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-09-15T06:18:47Z

## Languages

- CSS
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Python
- TypeScript
- Vue

## Top Contributors

- greentfrapp (594 contributions)

---

## README

# Panel

A research workspace where the agent works beside you: chat, files, PDFs and notebooks in one dock, and the agent can also create custom viewers and apps when necessary

This is an early build for testers. Expect rough edges, and feel free to raise issues.

Screenshot of Panel in action.

## Before you start

- Node 22.18 or newer (or 24.12 and newer)
- pnpm
- uv, which fetches the Python it needs (3.12 or newer) by itself
- Claude Code, installed and signed in: run `claude` once and log in. The agent and the literature review run through it.

## Install and start

```sh
pnpm install
uv sync
pnpm start
```

Then open. `pnpm start` builds the app first, so the first start takes a minute. Ctrl-C stops everything it started.

## Where your things are

- `~/Panel/panel.db` holds your conversations and everything the agents did.
- `~/Panel/workspaces` is where new Workspaces are created, unless you pick another folder.

Both are outside this folder, so deleting or re-cloning the repo keeps them.

## What works

- Chatting with an agent that can read and write files, and asks before running a tool.
- Workspaces: a folder the agent works in, with its own chats and saved layout.
- Panes for files, PDFs, markdown and Jupyter notebooks. Notebooks run against a real kernel, and you and the agent can edit the same one.
- Long-running commands in the background, which you can watch and stop.
- Panes the agent writes for you when you ask to see something a built-in Pane cannot show.
- A literature review: ask the chat for one, and open its result from the tool card.

## What doesn't yet

- Currently only has full support for Claude Code.
- Modules start only by asking the chat. There is no button to launch one.
- The hypothesis Modules have no view of their own, so their results can be hard to read.
- Modules don't work with OpenAI API yet.

## The OpenAI key (optional)

Copy `apps/server/.env.example` to `apps/server/.env` and set `OPENAI_API_KEY`. This adds "OpenAI API" to the agent picker, for chat and tools.

It does not run literature reviews or the hypothesis Modules: those need an agent that can search the web, and today only Claude Code can. Without a key, the picker shows OpenAI as not set up, which is expected.

## If something's wrong

- **"Panel couldn't reach its server."** The server half is not running. Check the terminal `pnpm start` is in, then press Retry.
- **An agent shows as not set up.** The reason is written under the message box.
- **A port is already in use**, or the app answers but never loads: run `pnpm dev:doctor`. It says what is holding each port and how to clear it.

## Licence

MIT

---

## The idea

### UI

The UI has multiple configurable windows, called Panes, that can display things ranging from image files, data files, code, as well as chat sessions. This is critical for researchers who often have to context switch between different types of files.

A default set of Panes are provided for common use cases. But custom Panes can also be added by humans and agents, such as a PDB viewer or SQLite visualizer.

### Module Protocol

Modules are similar to Skills but with additional definitions to support inter-module workflows and integration with the workspace.

Specifically, Modules have typed definitions for Inputs, Outputs, and Intermediates.

Inputs and Outputs are straightforward. Intermediates refer to objects that provide observability, such as the Chain-of-Thought or scratchpad for an agentic Module, or may be intermediate outputs in a multi-stage Module. These are especially important for processes that need transparency or long-running jobs that should show progress.

Having typed definitions for these enable validation at runtime and make it easier for humans and agents to develop custom Modules for downstream tasks and Panes for visualizations.

#### Data Abstraction Layer

A data abstraction layer (DAL) bridges in-memory and filesystem objects. A DAL helps to map a URI to either an in-memory store or a local file, so that the Module just has to concern itself with the manipulation of the object.


# Lume — open-source terminal: command blocks, AI, remote control

author: stagas

# stagas/livediff

A live Git diff view cli

- Stars: 9
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 9
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License

- Created: 2026-09-15T13:33:31Z

## Languages

- Shell

## Top Contributors

- stagas (2 contributions)

---

## README

# livediff

Stay on top of what your coding agents are doing with a live diff feed, right in
your terminal.

`livediff` watches the current Git repository and shows every edit as it happens,
whether it comes from an agent, an editor, or another tool. Changes appear like a
regular Git diff: added lines are green, removed lines are red, and unchanged
lines provide context. Each edit is shown once, keeping the feed focused on what
your agents are changing now.

## Install

Run this in your terminal:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stagas/livediff/main/install.sh | sh
```

The installer supports Linux and macOS on x64 or ARM64, and Windows x64 through
Git Bash. It downloads a standalone executable; only Git needs to be installed.

## Get started

Open a terminal in any Git repository and run:

```sh
livediff
```

Now edit and save a file. You will see output similar to:

```diff
diff --git a/example.ts b/example.ts 3:47:12 PM
--- a/example.ts
+++ b/example.ts
@@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
-const greeting = "Hello";
+const greeting = "Hello, world!";
```

Only edits made after `livediff` starts are displayed. It watches tracked files
and new files that are not excluded by your Git ignore rules.

Press `q` or Ctrl-C to stop.

## Compact mode

For a quieter view with only the filename, time, and changed lines, run:

```sh
livediff --compact
```

The short form works too:

```sh
livediff -c
```

Compact output looks like this:

```diff
example.ts 3:47:12 PM
-const greeting = "Hello";
+const greeting = "Hello, world!";
```

## Color and install location

Disable colors when redirecting output or using a terminal without color support:

```sh
NO_COLOR=1 livediff
```

The installer uses `/usr/local/bin` when it is writable and `~/.local/bin`
otherwise. To choose a different directory:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stagas/livediff/main/install.sh | INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/bin" sh
```

Release checksums are available as `SHA256SUMS` on the GitHub Releases page.

## Development

The project uses Go. To test or compile it from source:

```sh
go test ./...
go build -o dist/livediff .
```

MIT © 2026 stagas

title: Show HN: Ordewell – turn one goal into an ordered plan of coding-agent tasks
author: ac-ciano
body:
# ordewell/ordewell

Multi-agent task orchestration for coding agents. Turn one goal into an ordered plan of tasks — each with its own runner, model and mode — then execute and verify the results.

- Stars: 4
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 4
- Open issues: 0
- License: Other
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-07-31T15:20:40Z

## Languages

- CSS
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Shell
- TypeScript

## Top Contributors

- ac-ciano (10 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 Turn one goal into an ordered plan of coding-agent tasks — each with its own runner, model and mode — then execute and verify it. 
 

 
 Website ·
 Docs 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

---

## What this is

- **A plan you can rewrite before a token is spent.** The plan is a typed artifact, not an agent's internal state: every task carries a runner, model, thinking effort and mode, and you can change any of them, add and remove tasks, and rewire dependencies — without losing completed work or round-tripping the AI.
- **The right model per task, chosen in the open.** The planner makes one portfolio decision across the whole plan — a security refactor and a README update do not deserve the same model — and shows you every assignment before anything runs (why a separate planner?).
- **Verdicts from evidence, not opinion.** A task completes only when its unique completion marker appears in the runner's output; exit code is retained as diagnostic evidence. The model is never the tie-breaker. Stuck tasks can be advanced with *Mark complete*, and a task marked done by mistake goes back with *Mark not done*.
- **A planner that talks back.** Planning is one continuous chat: it researches your repo read-only, asks when your goal is vague, and its final message *is* the plan (ADR-0002). Reads run in parallel; anything reaching outside the workspace asks once; commands that would write are refused outright (ADR-0008).
- **No extra API key required.** Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode can *be* the planner, strictly read-only, on the subscription you already hold for the runners (ADR-0009).
- **Multi-runner by design.** Enable several and the planner assigns one per task. Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode ship built-in; anything else — Aider, your own CLI — is a plugin manifest, not a code change.

---

## Quick Start

Node.js ≥ 20 on macOS, Linux or Windows. The TUI also needs **tmux** — see
Platform support below.

```bash
npm install -g ordewell
ordewell                                       # the TUI — chat on the left, plan on the right
```

That's it. First run asks for a planner and a runner, set from inside
(`/planner`, `/runners`, `/key`) — no restart, no API key required up front.

`npx ordewell` works the same without a global install; the package also
ships scoped as `@ordewell/cli`.

For VS Code instead, install the extension — it carries its own core, so
there is nothing to install from npm:

```bash
code --install-extension ordewell.ordewell
```

Or search **Ordewell** in the Extensions view.

Building from source:
`git clone https://github.com/ordewell/ordewell.git && cd ordewell && npm install && npm run build && npm link -w packages/cli`
— see CONTRIBUTING.md.

### Scriptable / headless

Every slash command is also a subcommand — set the planner and runner by env
var to skip the TUI entirely.

**Already run Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode?** No separate API key — it
runs on the subscription you already hold:

```bash
export AI_PROVIDER="claude-code"        # or codex, opencode
ordewell plan --goal "Add rate limiting to the public API" && ordewell run
```

Mutation always stays with the runners; the planner agent only explores and
reasons. Same toggles apply from a UI: `/planner`, `/model`,
`/planner-effort`, or the planner bar in VS Code.

**Prefer an API key?** Twenty-five providers are recognised via their own
`*_API_KEY` — OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, xAI, Groq, DeepSeek,
Mistral, Together, Fireworks, Perplexity, Cerebras, DeepInfra, Cohere,
Novita, Kimi, Zhipu, Qwen, Doubao, Hunyuan, Baichuan, MiniMax, Yi, StepFun
and SiliconFlow. Run `ordewell key` for variable names, or point
`OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_BASE_URL` at anything else, including a local model
server.

```bash
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="sk-or-..."
ordewell plan --goal "Add rate limiting to the public API" && ordewell run
```

---

## Three surfaces, one core

### VS Code

A streaming timeline: live thinking, each research step with its outcome, and task cards you expand for the runner's own output. Retarget a task's runner and its model and mode re-derive in place. The whole loop is below, under **The VS Code loop, end to end**.

### Terminal UI

 

Everything the extension does, over SSH. `tab` swaps chat and plan pane; single keys drive the plan (`f` start, `E` run all, `m` toggle done, `R` runner, `o` model). `/help` lists the rest.

### CLI

```console
$ ordewell plan --goal "Add rate limiting to the public API"

Generating plan for: "Add rate limiting to the public API"...
✓ list_dir src → D middleware F router.ts F auth.ts
✓ grep X-RateLimit → no matches in 6 files

Question: should limits apply per API key, or per client IP?
My recommendation: per key — auth() already threads the key through req.ctx.
> per key, with an IP fallback for anonymous routes

Plan: 4 tasks (3 AI, 1 Manual) — claude-code, opencode
Session: session-1751600000000

   1. [ AI] Add a token-bucket limiter in src/middleware/rateLimit.ts (Claude Sonnet 4.5 · Claude Code)
   2. [ AI] Wire the limiter into route registration (Claude Haiku 4.5 · Claude Code)
   3. [ AI] Return RFC 6585 429s with Retry-After (DeepSeek V4 Flash · Opencode)
   4. [MAN] Document the limit headers in the OpenAPI spec

  [MAN] = manual step — run `ordewell tui` to work through it

  Run 'ordewell run' to execute, 'ordewell status' to inspect, or 'ordewell tui' for the full UI.

$ ordewell run
Executing plan...
  ✓ #a1b2 completed — PASS: Verified: completion marker detected in agent output. Task c
  ⟳ #c3d4 in_progress
[2/Wire the limiter into route registration] Started: claude-code / claude-haiku-4-5

Done. 4 completed, 0 failed, 0 blocked.
```

Every slash command is also an `ordewell` subcommand, so nothing is UI-only and headless automation reaches everything a human can.

---

## How it works

1. **Describe a goal** in plain prose.
2. **The planner researches** your workspace read-only and interleaves questions with research in one persistent conversation (ADR-0008).
3. **A plan appears** — ordered tasks, each with a runner, model, thinking effort and mode. Edit anything inline, or reprompt to reshape the whole plan without losing completed work.
4. **Execution** spawns a real coding-agent session per AI task, respecting the dependency graph and handing each task its predecessors' results. Manual tasks become checklists.
5. **The VerdictEngine** completes a task only once its marker appears; an exit without one fails visibly. Sessions auto-save to `.ordewell/sessions/`.

---

 
 Usage examples — planning, editing, multi-runner, plugins 

**Plan, edit, execute**

```bash
# The planner researches the repo and converses if the goal is underspecified
ordewell plan --goal "Migrate the config loader from JSON to TOML"

# Reassign before running — runner first, since it re-derives model, effort and mode
ordewell task-runner 2 opencode
ordewell task-deps 3 1,2

# Execute; independent tasks run in parallel (default: 3 concurrent sessions)
ordewell run

# Inspect any session later
ordewell status --session-id session-1751600000000
```

The surfaces differ only in how you name a target: the TUI opens a picker, the CLI takes an argument — and omitting the argument prints the same options the picker would have shown.

```bash
ordewell task-model 3            # lists the models that task's runner can spawn
ordewell task-model 3 sonnet     # picks one
```

**Configure without an editor**

```bash
ordewell planner claude-code     # plan on a coding agent's subscription — no API key
ordewell model set sonnet        # scoped to that agent's own catalog
ordewell planner-effort high     # a variant of the selected model
ordewell key set openrouter sk-… # stored in .env, never echoed back
ordewell runners codex off
```

Each pushes to the running server *before* writing `.env`, so the change lands on the next plan with no restart — and a refused connection cannot leave the file holding a setting the daemon never saw.

**Deep-interview planning with a PRD**

```bash
ordewell grill-me on   # planner interrogates your goal before outlining (min. 3 probing questions)
ordewell prd on        # planner previews, then writes a full PRD to .scratch/<slug>/PRD.md
ordewell tdd on        # tasks are augmented with red-green-refactor instructions

ordewell plan --goal "Real-time collaborative editing"
# → the planner grills you in chat, drafts the PRD, waits for your OK,
#   then commits the plan as its final message
```

**Multi-runner plans and custom runners**

```bash
# Pass --runner repeatedly to build a runner set; the planner assigns one per task
ordewell plan --goal "Refactor auth module" --runner claude-code --runner opencode

# Bring your own CLI agent via a plugin manifest
ordewell plugins create my-runner        # scaffolds manifest.json
ordewell plugins install github:user/repo
ordewell plugins list
```

**The other two front ends**

```bash
ordewell               # full-screen terminal UI — same as `ordewell tui`
ordewell web --daemon  # the local API server, in the background
```

`ordewell web` starts the HTTP + WebSocket API on `127.0.0.1:3742` that the CLI and TUI are clients of — every other command starts it for you on demand. It serves JSON, not a web page; there is no browser dashboard yet.

For VS Code, install the extension and open the Ordewell panel — see Quick Start.

| Area | Commands |
| --- | --- |
| Planning | type a goal, `/approve`, `/run`, `/stop` |
| Tasks | `/add-task`, `/remove-task`, `/complete`, `/uncomplete`, `/skip`, `/retry`, `/cancel`, `/force-start` |
| Skills | `/grill-me`, `/tdd`, `/prd`, `/review`, `/verify`, `/research-subagents` |
| Models | `/model`, `/key`, `/allowlist`, `/runners`, `/auto`, `/refresh` |
| Sessions | `/sessions`, `/new`, `/save`, `/load`, `/delete` — a loaded session is adopted by the server, so its plan stays executable |
| System | `/help`, `/mouse`, `/quit` |

API keys typed into `/key` are masked on screen and written to your `.env`.

Text is selectable and copyable with the mouse, as in any other program: Ordewell
does not capture the terminal's mouse. Scroll with `pgup`/`pgdn`. If you would
rather have wheel scrolling and can live without drag-to-select, `/mouse on`
swaps the trade (and remembers it via `ORDEWELL_TUI_MOUSE` in your `.env`).

A task's own terminal is a tmux window, where tmux does hold the mouse so the
wheel scrolls its scrollback. Selecting there still copies to your system
clipboard: drag to select and release to copy, or double/triple-click for a word
or a line. Install `wl-copy`, `xclip` or `xsel` on Linux if you have none of them
— without one, copying falls back to an OSC 52 escape that some terminals ignore.

 

 
 The VS Code loop, end to end — research, question, plan, execution, verdict 

 

 

 
 Platform support — including the Windows notes 

| Surface | Linux | macOS | Windows |
|---------|-------|-------|---------|
| VS Code extension | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| API server | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| CLI | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| TUI | ✅ needs tmux | ✅ needs tmux | needs tmux — run it under WSL |

**The TUI requires tmux on every platform**, not only Windows — it is what backs
each task's live terminal. Install it from your package manager (`apt install
tmux`, `brew install tmux`) before running `ordewell`. Everything else runs
natively on Windows: the planner (including harness planners), task execution,
model discovery, and the read-only exploration envelope all work there.

Two notes for Windows. Install the agent CLIs with their **native installers** where one exists — an npm-installed `claude`/`codex`/`opencode` is a `.cmd` shim, which has to start through cmd.exe and inherits its 8191-character command-line limit; that is fine for task prompts but not for the harness planner's larger system prompt, and Ordewell will tell you so by name rather than silently truncating it. And keep **Git for Windows** installed: its POSIX shell is what the planner runs research commands in, so `ls`, `cat`, `grep` and friends behave the same as they do everywhere else. See ADR-0010.

Any install route is found, on PATH or not: the PowerShell one-liner installers (`irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex`, OpenCode's equivalent), npm, pnpm, Yarn, bun, Scoop, Chocolatey, WinGet, and Volta. If a runner is greyed out in the picker right after you installed it, restart the VS Code window — a GUI-launched extension host holds the PATH it started with.

 

 
 Configuration — the four settings that matter 

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One provider key (`OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, …) | — | The one required setting. Twenty-five providers are recognised, each from its own variable — `ordewell key` lists them — plus any OpenAI-compatible endpoint via `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_BASE_URL`. The provider is auto-detected from whichever key is set (force with `AI_PROVIDER`). Not needed when `AI_PROVIDER` is `claude-code`, `codex`, or `opencode` — those plan with the CLI's own subscription. |
| `ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL` | `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` | The planner model — a budget model by default; it plans and researches but never writes code. Change via `ordewell model set ` or `/model`, which scope the choice to the planner backend's own catalog. With a coding-agent planner, it must be one of that agent's own model ids. |
| `ORDEWELL_PLANNER_EFFORT` | — | Thinking effort for a coding-agent planner, from the selected model's own variants (`low`, `high`, `adaptive`, …). Ignored by vendor planners, whose effort is baked into the model id. Change via `ordewell planner-effort ` or `/planner-effort`. |
| `ORDEWELL_MAX_PARALLEL` | `3` | Max concurrent AI task sessions (1–5). Independent tasks run in parallel; the dependency graph is always respected. |

Run `ordewell --help` for the full list of environment variables, or `ordewell setup` for the interactive wizard. VS Code users: everything is mirrored under `ordewell.*` settings.

 

 
 Architecture 

```text
packages/
├── core/    Pure TypeScript, zero UI deps — Session, PlanStore, Planner,
│            TaskOrchestrator, VerdictEngine, ModelResolver, ModeResolver,
│            RunnerRegistry + manifest template engine
├── cli/     ordewell: tui, plan, run, status, stop, web, models, setup,
│            plugins, grill-me, prd, tdd — plus tui/, a pure state +
│            renderer core behind a thin raw-mode terminal driver
├── vscode/  Extension + webview: streaming planner timeline, task cards,
│            TTY capture via script(1)
└── web/     Hono HTTP + WebSocket server — the local daemon the CLI and
             TUI drive over 127.0.0.1 (session pool, headless execution)
```

The TUI's core is pure — a reducer returning `{ state, effects }` and a renderer returning one string per terminal row (ADR-0006).

Tasks default to each runner's autonomous mode (toggle with `/auto`), and the plan is the source of truth for what runs — modes are never silently rewritten at spawn (ADR-0001).

Every surface consumes one event union (`SessionMessage`) over one broadcast seam — the domain vocabulary lives in CONTEXT.md and design decisions in docs/adr/.

 

 
 Acknowledgements 

The deep-interview planning workflows — `grill-me`, PRD drafting, TDD task augmentation, and review mode — are adapted from Matt Pocock's skills (MIT), rebuilt as prompt blocks inside Ordewell's planner and runner prompts. If you want those workflows in a plain coding-agent session rather than an orchestrated plan, his repo is the place to start.

 

---

## Contributing

Bug reports, feature requests and pull requests are welcome — start with CONTRIBUTING.md for the build order and the layout of the tree. Security issues go to SECURITY.md, not the public tracker.

New to the codebase? CONTEXT.md is the domain glossary and docs/adr/ records why things are the way they are.

Licensed under the Apache License 2.0. The Ordewell name and logos are not covered by that licence — see NOTICE.

For the projects I've done 35B Qwen is about the smallest that seems to make useful progress in a general purpose harness while 4B Qwen is workable with a task-specific harness. At the lower end the plan has to be traditional search/planner techniques in code not something the model has any control over, of course that limits the kinds of problems that fit. The high end coding models are perfectly capable of making a functional 1-off harness for those jobs so it ends up not being that bad to implement.

comments.text: I’ve had success with writing eg shell scripts that have a deterministic scaffold for the thing I’m actually trying to do, then call off to the agent for only the things that actually need it. For example I was trying to find a race condition flaky bug in my code, so the shell for loop ran the build N times, and called out to the agent to analyze the build logs if the tests failed, then the shell would ping me on slack when it was done, so the whole thing could run in the background.I’ve been thinking more about how this deterministic + agents style could work, it’s kinda like the analogy of factories in the 1800s going from the central shaft to electric motors on each desk (where the central shaft in this case is a chat window, and the motor on a desk is calling the llm api from wherever you want just like a normal api call)Of course, maybe in a few months the agents would just be reliable enough to do the shell part on their own too, but we’ll just have to wait and see

title: Show HN: An e-ink frame that hears birds and draws them as 1800s illustrations
author: arnemunthekaas
body:
# arnegiacomo/fugleramme

E-ink bird frame for Raspberry Pi - real-time bird detection by audio using BirdNET-Go

- Stars: 0
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 0
- Open issues: 5
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-07-08T19:01:49Z

## Languages

- Python
- Shell

## Topics

- bird-detection
- birding
- birdnet
- birdnet-go
- birdwatching
- e-ink
- inky-impression
- kiosk-software
- machine-learning
- raspberry-pi

## Top Contributors

- arnegiacomo (46 contributions)

---

## README

# fugleramme
E-ink bird frame for Raspberry Pi - real-time bird detection by audio.

Built on top of BirdNET-Go, which runs
the mic and the BirdNET classifier and owns all detection config. Fugleramme reads
its detections and renders the recently-seen birds as a collage on an Inky-Impression e-ink panel, and serves the same view as a web kiosk.

## Art

The birds are cut-outs from historic, public-domain natural-history drawings,
hand-curated for this project. Each detected species is matched to its
illustration, background-removed, and packed onto a textured paper page - larger
birds toward the centre, sized by real body mass. Species with no illustration
are currently left off, and an empty window shows a bare perch.

| No detections | A few visitors | A full garden |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| No birds detected | A few garden birds | Many garden birds |

## Run locally

```bash
uv sync                                       # set up venv
uv run python -m fugleramme.seed --count 40   # seed db (no BirdNET-Go in dev)
uv run fugleramme-frame                       # start service on :8080
uv run fugleramme-dev                         # same as above with hot-reload
```

Open the kiosk (no SPI-panel needed):

```bash
open -na "Google Chrome" --args --kiosk --app=http://localhost:8080/
```

## Run on a Raspberry Pi

Clone the repo on the Pi and run the idempotent one-command bootstrap:

```bash
./setup.sh          # add -y to auto-accept dependency installs (uv, docker, etc...)
```

It installs any missing deps, brings up BirdNET-Go (container + mic), and enables
the frame as a systemd service that pushes to the Inky panel and serves the kiosk
on `:8080`. Details: `detector/README.md`. 

Want to update? Just pull and run ./setup.sh again

## License

- Code (`wikimedia-scrape/`, application code): MIT - see `LICENSE`.
- Bird images (`assets/birds/`): CC BY-SA 4.0 - see
 `assets/birds/ATTRIBUTION.md`.
- Bird sizes (`assets/bird_sizes.csv`): body mass from AVONET (Tobias et al.
 2022, Ecology Letters, doi:10.1111/ele.13898),
 CC BY 4.0.

comments.author: arnemunthekaas
comments.text: Author here. A mic listens to the sounds in my garden, BirdNET-Go (an open-source BirdNET classifier) detects birds by sound, and the e-ink frame draws a real 1800s natural-history illustration of each one as it hears them. Here’s a live web-demo from my garden in Bergen, Norway: https://fugleramme.arnegiacomo.devA few things that might be interesting:- The screen only redraws when the set of birds changes, and dithers the collage down to six colours for the e-ink display.- Bigger birds sit toward the centre, scaled by real body mass.- 800+ cutouts across 400+ species, each cut from a real public domain plate. All art is historic and human-made. Coverage is currently best for the Nordics, Britain and Germany (but other parts of the world are in the works).- Runs fully local on a Raspberry Pi or your homelab (yes, even the classifier runs great on a RPI)The e-ink panel is optional and it can run web-only in a container against a BirdNET-Go you already have.Happy to answer any questions!

comments.author: lambda
comments.text: There are LLMs that support audio input, similar to those with vision support.From my testing of open weights LLMs with audio support, they basically are only trained to recognize audio as an alternative to text input, they treat audio as basically equivalent to a transcript, and can't recognize or distinguish things like music, accents, background sounds, etc.So they're only really good for transcribing or summarizing or using audio input in place of text input for prompts, but not anything that requires distinguishing any information about the audio that would not be present in a transcript.It can be tempting to try to use an LLM for a variety of tasks; kind of the whole thing about an LLM is that you don't have to do a separate complex training run for every task, but can just provide instructions in natural language. But it only works as far as what the training data covers, if the training basically always treated audio and a text transcript as equivalent, the model has nothing causing it to learn other relevant features of the audio. If there's enough bird call identification in the training data of an LLM, it might be able to do that, but I think multimodal training data tends to be much more limited than the text training corpus

title: Show HN: Breathe CLI – Paced resonance breathing in the macOS terminal
author: marekkowalczyk
body: I built a terminal app that paces slow breathing at 6 breaths per minute for vagal tone training. It's a single Python file, stdlib only, no dependencies — just run breathe and follow the bar.I'm a cardiology patient (HFrEF). Slow breathing at resonance frequency is one of the few non-pharmacological interventions shown to improve cardiac vagal tone and baroreflex sensitivity (Bernardi et al., Circulation 2002; Lancet 1998). I wanted a frictionless daily habit tool — no app store, no account, no subscription, just open terminal and go.Design constraints, all grounded in the clinical literature:- No breath retention — Valsalva risk in cardiac patients- No rapid breathing — minimum 8-second cycles- Exhale ≤ 2x inhale — no evidence for extreme ratios- Immediate exit, always — q or Ctrl+C restores the terminal even on crashThe README includes a resonance frequency measurement protocol for anyone with a chest-strap HRV monitor who wants to find their individual optimum instead of using the 6 bpm default.macOS only (uses afplay for audio cues). MIT licensed.pip install breathe-cliorbrew tap marekkowalczyk/breathe && brew install breathe.

title: Show HN: Jynx, a matchmaking app to find gaming teammates
author: akiro____
body:
TL;DR: Jynx is a gaming social platform that matches you with compatible teammates based on skill level, play style and schedule. Swipe to find players (Tinder-style), create or join game sessions (LFG), chat, and build your squad. 214k lines of Dart, 23 feature modules, built entirely with Claude Code as my entry into agentic engineering.Live on App Store and Play Store:
https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=app.jynx
https://apps.apple.com/fr/app/jynx-where-gaming-gets-social/...---Hi HN, long time lurker, first time poster, be gentle.Developer by day, vibe coder by night: Jynx is the project I used to ease into agentic engineering.AI talks are mitigated, at best. But I'll talk about my experience here. Forgive my erratic style, it is what it is.Working with Claude from the very beginning, it's been a blast. I had the "chance" to have the time necessary to learn and use AI a lot. Lots of different techniques that quickly became completely obsolete today.Without LLMs, it would have been extremely hard to have the same app than I have today. I used Flutter (Dart) to avoid having to dev and maintain two codebases. It is not a language I knew. Learning the language first would have severely hindered the process.For me, from copy/paste to using MCP then Roo Code, then Claude Code was an ecstatic process. I always loved having ideas but the time it would take me to build the thing and test it always felt too long. Not anymore.So we carefully designed, iterated and implemented the two codebases for Jynx. One for the flutter app, one for the firebase backend. I chose Firebase to avoid having to maintain a server and be able to focus on the UI/UX of the app.We started thinking about it in December 2024 and started devs early 2025; not working on it full time at all. We really poured our heart into it and we truly tried to make it as secure as possible. Even though we mean business, it is a passion project. By using the excuse of learning agentic flows, I took the time to inspect each aspects of the app's systems thoroughly.Tech stack:
- Flutter 3.41 / Dart 3.11 (single codebase, iOS + Android)
- Firebase (Firestore, Cloud Functions in TypeScript, Auth, Storage, FCM)
- Riverpod 3.1 + Freezed + json_serializable for state management & immutable models
- Drift for encrypted local SQLite caching (offline-first architecture to optimize Firebase costs)
- Clean Architecture with feature modules and mixin-based repositories
- Sentry + Firebase Crashlytics for production error reporting
- Freerasp for runtime app self-protection (tamper detection, root/jailbreak)Agentic engineering artifacts:
- Claude Code (Claude + GLM) as primary coding agent
- 22 hooks, 18 skills, 13 instincts, 8 rule files, custom subagents, slash commands, MCP servers and plugins (instincts system from Affaan's https://github.com/affaan-m/everything-claude-code)
- GitNexus
- MemPalace for persistent context across sessionsStats: 1,239 Dart files, 214k lines of code (excluding generated boilerplate), 30k lines of comments across the Flutter codebase.I made a detailed cheatsheet document about my whole setup if you want it. I could post it or you DM me.If you have questions, ask away, I'll gladly answer.Test it and tell me what you think of it honestly, I won't get offended!Take care,
Antoine

title: Show HN: Claude-account – switch Claude Code accounts without logging in again
author: hamza_rehman
body:
I use separate Claude Code accounts for work and personal projects. Having to log out and go through the login flow every time I switched accounts became annoying, so I built a small CLI to solve it.The commands are intentionally simple:claude account add myworkaccount
claude account add mypersonalaccount
claude account use myworkaccount
claude account currentAfter switching, Claude Code works normally:claude
claude "fix this bug in main.py"

title: Show HN: TurboGPT: train 22KiB transformer in 13s
author: lostmsu
body:
# lostmsu/TurboGPT

Train a tiny GPT in under a minute (CUDA only)

- Stars: 35
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 35
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: master
- Created: 2026-09-23T20:21:23Z

## Languages

- C++
- Cuda
- Nix
- PowerShell
- Python

## Top Contributors

- lostmsu (9 contributions)

---

## README

# turboGPT

Tiny byte-level GPT training in CUDA C++. MIT.

## Build

Linux/NixOS:

```bash
nix-build -o build/nix-result
```

Windows, Visual Studio 2022 C++ tools, and CUDA 13.4:

```powershell
.\build.ps1 -CudaArch 86
```

`CudaArch` is the GPU compute capability from NVIDIA's CUDA GPU list.

## Run

```powershell
.\build\turbogpt.exe --data hn1g.txt --log-to runs/ctx4
```

The run stores its checkpoint at
`runs/ctx4/ctx4.pt`, containing model, optimizer, scheduler, and trainer state.
Use `--load CHECKPOINT.pt` to resume it.

`runs/ctx4/report.json` is derived from the log directory. Logs are TensorBoard-compatible:
one report per batch, capped at 8Mi reports, and flushed with periodic or final checkpoints.

## Result

- hn1g after 1.5G training tokens: **2.5295 BPB**.

## Tests

```powershell
python tests\verify.py
```
